Dell PowerScale: Added support of revert to snapshot

This change adds revert-to-snapshot support to the Dell PowerScale
Manila driver. When revert_to_snapshot_support is enabled in the share
type, the driver creates a Domain Mark job during share creation and
uses asynchronous SnapRevert jobs for the actual revert operation.

The driver returns STATUS_REVERTING_TO_SNAPSHOT and relies on the
periodic task in the share manager (from the core change) to poll
the backend job status via get_share_status.

Configuration options:
- powerscale_job_retries: Max polling attempts (default: 5)
- powerscale_job_interval: Polling interval in seconds (default: 2)

revisions.message:
Support deploy amphora in different availability zones

- Added option to enable multizone deployment in Octavia config
  Enabling this option changes behaviour for creation Amphora in
  availability zones (more detailes below).
- Added attribute for octavia availability zones, which indicates, that
  AZ could be used in multizone deployment.
- Added attribute for amphora resource to indicate, which AZ was
  calculated in multizone deployment.
- Added validation to create Loadbalancer with multizone enabled flag,
  but without configured AZ. It's not allowed to do.
- Main logic is placed in ComputeCreate task.

Key ideas:
- Now Octavia AZ could be marked as available for multizone usage.
- After enabling multizone in config marked octavia AZ will be used for
  creation amphora desributed in these AZs.
- If NO AZ available (marked for multizone), the default config option
  will be used.
  It's done for compatible with non multizone mode.
- If multizone mode enabled and availability zone is specified on API
  request directly - it will ignore multizone logic and creates all
  amphora in the same target AZ. Also it will continue work in the same
  way in failover, i.e. amphora will be re-created in the same AZ.
  It's done for compatible with non multizone mode.
- AZ should have "compute_zone" and "volume_zone" to be marked as
  available for multizone deployment.

Important: Octavia with with the same compute_zone handled as one AZ,
because administrator could configure several AZ like:
az1:        compute_zone - Z1, volume_zone - Z1
az1_extra:  compute_zone - Z1, volume_zone - Z1_extra

And in this case will be incorrect to desctribute Amphoras in the same
compute AZ, because we want to provide different AZ for compute zones
firstly.

In deployment with enabled multizone AZ for amphora will be calculated
on creation Loadbalancer and on Failover LB/Amphora. The logic is
following:
- Group octavia AZs by uniq compute zones.
- Find AZ index for master/single amphora by loadbalancer id hash like:
  idx = hash(lb_id) % len(uniq_compute_zones)
- Get compute AZ from group on first step. Take first octavia AZ
  associated with this compute AZ - it will be a AZ for master/single
  amphora.
- For Backup amphora use random octavia AZ, exclude octavia AZs with the
  same compute_zone as for Master amphora.
  If there no such AZs - the same AZ as for Master amphora will be used.

OR if AZ is already specified for amphora:
- take AZ fro amphora and check, that this AZ is enabled and marked for
  multizone.
- if it's true - use this AZ
- otherwise re-calculate AZ. BUT do not update AZ in amphora
  description, to allow creation amphora in "correct" zone after turning
  this AZ back.

The biggest part of PR is 1.5 k lines of tests for CreateCompute task.
It covers the ollowing cases:
* Creation Amphora with Single and Active Standby topologies
* Failover Loadbalancer or Separate Amphora in Single and Active Standby
  topologies.
* Failover with different count of available AZ
* Failover old LB (created before enabling multizone setup)
* Failover LB after enabling multizone, when AZ is already calculated
  for amphora

Note, that current PR uses some ideas from
https://review.opendev.org/c/openstack/octavia/+/923939.
- Make decision based on Task name, i.e. identify amphora role and
  current flow: creation or failover.
- During failover search Amphora role in Loadbalancer amphoras based on
  status PENDING_DELETE.

Change-Id: Id391e43752c7d952ed3703275ee5d06ffbf038d6

Signed-off-by: Sergey Kraynev <sergejyit@gmail.com>
Change-Id: I96a6d019aef823f5c13918bce874a88d008c53b9

  Enabling this option changes behaviour for creation Amphora in
  availability zones (more detailes below).
- Added attribute for octavia availability zones, which indicates, that
  AZ could be used in multizone deployment.
- Added attribute for amphora resource to indicate, which AZ was
  calculated in multizone deployment.
- Added validation to create Loadbalancer with multizone enabled flag,
  but without configured AZ. It's not allowed to do.
- Main logic is placed in ComputeCreate task.

Key ideas:
- Now Octavia AZ could be marked as available for multizone usage.
- After enabling multizone in config marked octavia AZ will be used for
  creation amphora desributed in these AZs.
- If NO AZ available (marked for multizone), the default config option
  will be used.
  It's done for compatible with non multizone mode.
- If multizone mode enabled and availability zone is specified on API
  request directly - it will ignore multizone logic and creates all
  amphora in the same target AZ. Also it will continue work in the same
  way in failover, i.e. amphora will be re-created in the same AZ.
  It's done for compatible with non multizone mode.
- AZ should have "compute_zone" and "volume_zone" to be marked as
  available for multizone deployment.

Important: Octavia with with the same compute_zone handled as one AZ,
because administrator could configure several AZ like:
az1:        compute_zone - Z1, volume_zone - Z1
az1_extra:  compute_zone - Z1, volume_zone - Z1_extra

And in this case will be incorrect to desctribute Amphoras in the same
compute AZ, because we want to provide different AZ for compute zones
firstly.

In deployment with enabled multizone AZ for amphora will be calculated
on creation Loadbalancer and on Failover LB/Amphora. The logic is
following:
- Group octavia AZs by uniq compute zones.
- Find AZ index for master/single amphora by loadbalancer id hash like:
  idx = hash(lb_id) % len(uniq_compute_zones)
- Get compute AZ from group on first step. Take first octavia AZ
  associated with this compute AZ - it will be a AZ for master/single
  amphora.
- For Backup amphora use random octavia AZ, exclude octavia AZs with the
  same compute_zone as for Master amphora.
  If there no such AZs - the same AZ as for Master amphora will be used.

OR if AZ is already specified for amphora:
- take AZ fro amphora and check, that this AZ is enabled and marked for
  multizone.
- if it's true - use this AZ
- otherwise re-calculate AZ. BUT do not update AZ in amphora
  description, to allow creation amphora in "correct" zone after turning
  this AZ back.

The biggest part of PR is 1.5 k lines of tests for CreateCompute task.
It covers the ollowing cases:
* Creation Amphora with Single and Active Standby topologies
* Failover Loadbalancer or Separate Amphora in Single and Active Standby
  topologies.
* Failover with different count of available AZ
* Failover old LB (created before enabling multizone setup)
* Failover LB after enabling multizone, when AZ is already calculated
  for amphora

Note, that current PR uses some ideas from
https://review.opendev.org/c/openstack/octavia/+/923939.
- Make decision based on Task name, i.e. identify amphora role and
  current flow: creation or failover.
- During failover search Amphora role in Loadbalancer amphoras based on
  status PENDING_DELETE.

Add availability_zones (plural) API for load balancer creation

Allow users to explicitly specify a list of availability zones for
amphora distribution when creating a load balancer. This complements
the existing availability_zone (singular) parameter and the automatic
multizone selection.

The new availability_zones parameter is mutually exclusive with
availability_zone. Each zone in the list must exist, be enabled, and
have use_in_multizone=True. A junction table
(load_balancer_availability_zone) stores the LB-to-AZ associations.

During LB creation, the controller worker selects master and backup
AZs from the explicit list. During failover, AZ candidates are
restricted to the explicit list when present.

restricted to the explicit list when present.

Deploy Kerbside with Kolla-Ansible.

This change implements the Kerbside Kolla-Ansible deployment role. It is a
fairly large change, but I couldn't find a meaningful way to break it up
into smaller chunks.

The basic idea is that there is a proxy sitting in front of the Nova
hypervisors that can talk the SPICE protocol to clients, lookup where the
console is on the relevant hypervisor, and then build a SPICE connection
to that hypervisor. It then shovels SPICE packets back and forth between
the two.

That proxy is called Kerbside and it consists of two components which
each have their own Kolla container. kerbside-api handles business logic
and is a uwsgi app. kerbside-proxy is the SPICE native component. Because
kerbside-proxy is not talking HTTP to clients, and expects TLS encrypted
traffic on the secure port, it uses the frontend certificates to do TLS
itself, and haproxy simply acts as a layer four load balancer.

Change-Id: I73a7a0b521085fd4023b08ab6f8a137d53a8712a
Depends-On: https://review.opendev.org/c/openstack/kolla/+/975495
Closes-Bug: #2131793
Signed-off-by: Michael Still <mikal@stillhq.com>

Deploy Kerbside with Kolla-Ansible.

This change implements the Kerbside Kolla-Ansible deployment role. It is a
fairly large change, but I couldn't find a meaningful way to break it up
into smaller chunks.

The basic idea is that there is a proxy sitting in front of the Nova
hypervisors that can talk the SPICE protocol to clients, lookup where the
console is on the relevant hypervisor, and then build a SPICE connection
to that hypervisor. It then shovels SPICE packets back and forth between
the two.

That proxy is called Kerbside and it consists of two components which
each have their own Kolla container. kerbside-api handles business logic
and is a uwsgi app. kerbside-proxy is the SPICE native component. Because
kerbside-proxy is not talking HTTP to clients, and expects TLS encrypted
traffic on the secure port, it uses the frontend certificates to do TLS
itself, and haproxy simply acts as a layer four load balancer.

This change implements the Kerbside Kolla-Ansible deployment role. It is a
fairly large change, but I couldn't find a meaningful way to break it up
into smaller chunks.

The basic idea is that there is a proxy sitting in front of the Nova
hypervisors that can talk the SPICE protocol to clients, lookup where the
console is on the relevant hypervisor, and then build a SPICE connection
to that hypervisor. It then shovels SPICE packets back and forth between
the two.

That proxy is called Kerbside and it consists of two components which
each have their own Kolla container. kerbside-api handles business logic
and is a uwsgi app. kerbside-proxy is the SPICE native component. Because
kerbside-proxy is not talking HTTP to clients, and expects TLS encrypted
traffic on the secure port, it uses the frontend certificates to do TLS
itself, and haproxy simply acts as a layer four load balancer.

revisions.message:
Add Gunicorn using gthreads as wsgi server

If you want to run Swift without eventlet you need to set the
environment variable "USE_EVENTLET=0". For example, using swift-init:

        USE_EVENTLET=0 swift-init restart main

You can also uninstall eventlet before (re-)starting the Swift services
to ensure it is working without it.

Due to a more strict validation of requests, headers and different
encoding a bit of monkey patching is required to match the current
behaviour running Swift with eventlet.

To tune gunicorns a new setting "threads" has been added to the
*-server.conf files. It defaults to 4, but especially the proxy-server
and object-server might be more performant using a higher setting. Note
that this is the number of threads per worker; the number of workers is
by default set to the number of CPU-cores.

Functional tests (still requiring eventlet at this point) should pass
with this implementation, except for the xprofile middleware which
depends on eventlet.

This implementation does not yet work with EC; this needs additional
changes to support 100-Continue requests and will be added in a
followup.

by default set to the number of CPU-cores.

revisions.message:
Stop looking for remote index with wheels

When we are building wheels, we do not need to check remote index from
containers at all, as all expected packages are expected to be present
on repo containers.

At the moment pip also checks remote index for each package when
searching for versions, which adds overhead and execution time.

Tests on placement role showed, that execution time has reduced around 7
seconds for the venv rebuild solely.

Change-Id: Id399c4440e8b66ae47a07bb14c9246fa610f45dd
Signed-off-by: Dmitriy Rabotyagov <dmitriy.rabotyagov@cleura.com>

Use PEP503 Simple Repository format for wheels

When we are building wheels, we do not need to check remote index from
containers at all, as all expected packages are expected to be present
on repo containers.

With that, current proces of find-links takes quite some extra time
to look for wheel content, producing series of requests toward both
the local repo container, but also remote PyPi index.

In order to limit external communication along with removing overhead,
we are forming wheels according to PEP 503 Simple Index, while keeping
backwards compatability.
Wheels inside of the simple folder are symlinks to old wheels folder.

Change-Id: Id399c4440e8b66ae47a07bb14c9246fa610f45dd
Signed-off-by: Dmitriy Rabotyagov <dmitriy.rabotyagov@cleura.com>

revisions.message:
Add kerbside CI scenario jobs.

Adds three non-voting Zuul jobs that deploy kolla-ansible AIO with
enable_kerbside set to true on Debian Trixie, Ubuntu Noble, and Rocky
10. The jobs follow the masakari scenario layout: a base job that
sets scenario: kerbside, three distro-specific jobs using the
existing single-node 16GB AIO nodesets, and a project-template
collecting them under check (not gate) while the jobs are still
being shaken down.

The jobs trigger via files: !inherit on changes to kerbside and
nova roles and group_vars, plus the kerbside-specific cert
files. globals-default.j2 gets a {% if scenario == "kerbside" %}
block that enables kerbside and sets nova_console to spice.
tests/run.yml is extended so openstack_core_tested includes the
kerbside scenario, which causes init-core-openstack.sh and the
kolla-ansible-tempest role to run with the default .*smoke.* regex
inherited from the base job.

The base job sets kolla_build_images: true with a 10800 second
timeout to match the existing non-voting image-building jobs (the
SPICE-enabled kolla images are not yet in the published image set,
so kerbside CI builds them locally). Combined with a Depends-On
line in the Gerrit submission pointing at the matching kolla
change, this gives Zuul speculative execution end-to-end: the
depended-on kolla patch is applied to the kolla source tree on
the test node, images are built from it and pushed to the local
primary:4000 registry, and the need_build_image branch of
globals-default.j2 flips docker_namespace and docker_registry to
use that registry.

Future work: add kerbside-specific Tempest tests via a plugin and
extend kolla_ansible_tempest_regex once the smoke baseline is
trusted.

Prompt: Michael asked me to draft the new tempest test in
src/kolla-ansible/ and then commit it here so he can produce a
patch from the resulting diff. A follow-up asked to enable
image-building plus the timeout bump used by the existing
non-voting image-building kolla-ansible jobs, so the kerbside
scenario can exercise an in-flight kolla change via Depends-On.

Assisted-By: Claude Opus 4.7 (1M context, medium effort) <noreply@anthropic.com>
Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.7 (1M context, medium effort) <noreply@anthropic.com>

subject: Add kerbside CI scenario jobs.

revisions.message:
Run the spice-direct tempest test in the kerbside scenario.

The kerbside scenario jobs added in I1784562d already deploy
kolla-ansible with enable_kerbside=yes and nova_console=spice, then
run the default ".*smoke.*" Tempest regex. This adds the SPICE
coverage that motivated the scenario in the first place.

The test itself lives in upstream Tempest as
tempest.api.compute.admin.test_spice.SpiceDirectConsoleTestJSON
and exercises the full spice-direct console flow: create an
instance, request a console token, exchange it for hypervisor
connection details, and complete a SPICE protocol handshake
against the returned hypervisor host:port. It skips itself unless
CONF.compute_feature_enabled.spice_console is True, and nothing
in kolla-ansible currently sets that — python-tempestconf does
not auto-detect SPICE from the cloud.

Two changes are needed:

1. roles/kolla-ansible-tempest gains a new
   kolla_ansible_tempest_discover_overrides list, whose entries
   are appended as positional "section.option value" arguments to
   discover-tempest-config. This is the same override syntax the
   role already uses for compute.build_timeout, so no new code
   path is introduced — just a per-scenario knob.

2. zuul.d/scenarios/kerbside.yaml sets that override to enable
   compute-feature-enabled.spice_console and extends
   kolla_ansible_tempest_regex so the spice test is selected
   alongside the existing smoke tests. The test has no smoke
   decorator, so without this it would be discovered but not
   run.

Note that this test _does_not_ validate that Kerbside is deployed
and working correctly. That's the next step after this one.

Prompt: Michael asked for a follow-up patch to patch156 that
actually runs the spice-direct Tempest test (originally added to
Tempest for Nova's CI) inside the kerbside scenario.

subject: Run the spice-direct tempest test in the kerbside scenario.

revisions.message:
Run a Kerbside-fronted SPICE tempest test in the kerbside scenario.

Patch157 enabled the upstream spice-direct test, which speaks SPICE
to the hypervisor port Nova returns. That validates Nova's
spice-direct plumbing but does not exercise Kerbside at all. This
adds a follow-up test that proves the URL Nova returns is fronted
by Kerbside's haproxy and that Kerbside is answering as SPICE.

The test lives in the kerbside-tempest-plugin, a separate releasable
in the shakenfist/kerbside repository whose version is tied to
Kerbside's via setuptools_scm. The plugin contributes one test,
kerbside_tempest_plugin.tests.api.test_spice_via_kerbside, which:

1. Calls Nova's get-remote-console with spice-direct/spice.
2. HTTPS-GETs the returned URL using the Kolla-Ansible CA
   (/etc/kolla/certificates/ca/root.crt by default), which is the
   trust chain for the haproxy front-end Kerbside terminates.
3. Parses the .vv file Kerbside serves at that URL, extracts the
   SPICE host, tls-port, and embedded CA certificate.
4. Opens a TLS connection to that host:tls-port trusting only the
   embedded CA, sends a SpiceLinkMess for the main channel, and
   reads back the SpiceLinkReply header. A SPICE magic in the reply
   proves Kerbside is talking SPICE.

The test does not yet authenticate or route through to a hypervisor
console -- that needs the auth ticket from the .vv file and a fuller
walk of the SPICE protocol, which will land separately backed by
shakenfist/ryll and shakenfist/uncalibrated-sextant.

Three changes are needed in kolla-ansible:

1. roles/kolla-ansible-tempest gains a new kolla_ansible_tempest_plugins
   list. Entries are appended to the pip install of the tempest venv,
   so callers can install tempest plugins from PyPI, git URLs, or
   local paths.

2. zuul.d/scenarios/kerbside.yaml uses that list to install
   kerbside-tempest-plugin from the shakenfist/kerbside repo,
   pulling from the develop branch.

3. The same scenario file extends kolla_ansible_tempest_regex so the
   new test is selected alongside the existing smoke set and the
   spice-direct test added in patch157.

Prompt: Michael asked for a follow-up to patch157 that runs a
tempest test through the Kerbside haproxy front-end, after we
discussed whether to ship it as an in-tree patch against tempest or
as a separate tempest plugin. We landed on a plugin in the kerbside
repo, packaged as its own releasable but sharing kerbside's version
via a setuptools_scm root pointing at the parent directory.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.7 (1M context, medium effort) <noreply@anthropic.com>

revisions.message:
Support cold migration with virtiofs shares

Cold migration was blocked for instances with virtiofs
share attachments because Nova never granted Manila
access or mounted shares on the destination host.

This change lifts that restriction with a lazy cleanup
strategy: shares stay mounted on the source until confirm.
On the destination, _finish_resize() grants Manila access
and mounts shares before calling the driver. Revert cleans
up the destination; the source retains its mounts
throughout.

New helpers _grant_share_access() and _revoke_share_access()
encapsulate Manila access operations without side effects
(no status transitions, notifications, or DB changes).
The existing allow_share()/deny_share() are refactored to
call these helpers.

The @block_shares_not_supported() decorator on resize() is
replaced with an inline SERVICE_VERSION 73 check, gating
cold migration on all computes supporting it.

The share_info parameter is added to finish_migration() and
finish_revert_migration() in the base driver, libvirt,
VMware, and fake drivers so the destination can include
virtiofs filesystems in the domain XML.

Partially-implements: blueprint virtiofs-cold-migration
Signed-off-by: Goutham Pacha Ravi <gouthampravi@gmail.com>
Assisted-by: Claude Opus 4.6
Change-Id: I2cda35fa0c2e080a67418d557cb9030b11f31394

Support cold migration with virtiofs shares

Lift the restriction on cold migration and resize for
instances with virtiofs share attachments. On the
destination, _finish_resize() grants Manila access and
mounts shares. Revert cleans up the destination; the
source retains its mounts until confirm. Same-host resize
skips redundant grant/mount/unmount/revoke operations.

A two-layer gate controls access: API microversion 2.104
signals client support, and SERVICE_VERSION 73 ensures
all computes can handle cold migration with shares.

Change-Id: I2cda35fa0c2e080a67418d557cb9030b11f31394

Support cold migration with virtiofs shares

Lift the restriction on cold migration and resize for
instances with virtiofs share attachments. On the
destination, _finish_resize() grants Manila access and
mounts shares. Revert cleans up the destination; the
source retains its mounts until confirm. Same-host resize
skips redundant grant/mount/unmount/revoke operations.

mount_all() now calls grant_access() before each mount,
so recovery paths (hard reboot, stop/start) re-establish
Manila access without operator intervention.

A two-layer gate controls access: API microversion 2.105
signals client support, and SERVICE_VERSION 73 ensures
all computes can handle cold migration with shares.

Partially-implements: blueprint virtiofs-cold-migration
Depends-On: I35738e2280e18b62564a90fdbda32e86fe5f179f

s3api: User Checksum Persistence on MPUs

Swift does checksum validation on UploadPart during an
Multi-Part Object Upload, but it does not presist that checksum
metadata after.

See AWS Docs:
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/checking-object-integrity-upload.html

s3api: User Checksum Persistence on MPUs

Swift does checksum validation on UploadPart during an
Multi-Part Object Upload, but it does not presist that checksum
metadata after.

Like checksum persistence on full object uploads,
This patch allows users of the s3api to specify a checksum
algorithm during a Multi Part Upload of both
FULL_OBJECT checksum types and also COMPOSITE checksum types.
A user can also just test checksums on UploadPart requests
instead of the entire MPU lifecycle.

We persist s3api sysmeta headers on the MPU manifest
and use that to decide what checksum algorithm to
enforce in later stages of the MPU lifecycle, and how
to validate the final checksum. We also use checksum
metadata from override headers in 'content-type' to
get metadata during listing of MPU parts.

This patch does not add support for checksum computation
for UploadPartCopy when the Copy Source does not have or
match the checksum algorithm on the MPU.

See AWS Docs:
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/checking-object-integrity-upload.html

s3api: User Checksum Persistence on MPUs

Swift does checksum validation on UploadPart during an
Multi-Part Object Upload, but it does not presist that checksum
metadata after.

Like checksum persistence on full object uploads,
This patch allows users of the s3api to specify a checksum
algorithm during a Multi Part Upload of both
FULL_OBJECT checksum types and also COMPOSITE checksum types.
A user can also just insert specific checksums on UploadPart requests
instead the same checksum on each part the entire MPU lifecycle.

We persist s3api sysmeta headers on the MPU manifest
and use that to decide what checksum algorithm to
enforce in later stages of the MPU lifecycle, and how
to validate the final checksum for the MPU.

This patch does not add support for checksum computation
for UploadPartCopy when the Copy Source does not have or
match the checksum algorithm on the MPU.

The S3 API behavior changes for multipart uploads:

* CreateMultipartUpload accepts x-amz-checksum-algorithm and
  x-amz-checksum-type, persists the selected checksum configuration,
  and returns both values in the response.
* UploadPart validates and persists x-amz-checksum-* values and returns
  the validated checksum in the response. Checksum-aware uploads
  require each part to use the algorithm selected at initiation.
* UploadPartCopy preserves and returns the source checksum when copying
  the complete source object with a compatible checksum algorithm.
* CompleteMultipartUpload persists and returns the completed checksum
  and checksum type. GetObject and HeadObject return these values when
  x-amz-checksum-mode: ENABLED is requested.
* COMPOSITE checksums support CRC32, CRC32C, SHA1, and SHA256.
  FULL_OBJECT checksums support CRC32, CRC32C, and CRC64NVME.
* UploadPartCopy requests and incompatible source checksums return 501.

See AWS Docs:
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/checking-object-integrity-upload.html

s3api: User Checksum Persistence on MPUs

Swift does checksum validation on UploadPart during a
Multi-Part Object Upload, but it does not persist that checksum
metadata after.

Like checksum persistence on full object uploads,
This patch allows users of the s3api to specify a checksum
algorithm during a Multi Part Upload of both
FULL_OBJECT checksum types and also COMPOSITE checksum types.
A user can also just insert specific checksums on UploadPart requests
instead the same checksum on each part the entire MPU lifecycle.

We persist s3api sysmeta headers on the MPU manifest
and use that to decide what checksum algorithm to
enforce in later stages of the MPU lifecycle, and how
to validate the final checksum for the MPU.

During CompleteMultipartUpload, SLO gathers each segment’s
checksum metadata and passes the aligned HEAD response headers
to s3api’s manifest hook. s3api validates the stored part checksums
against any client-provided values, calculates and validates
the completed MPU checksum, and persists the resulting checksum
metadata on the final SLO manifest using the footer callback.

This patch does not add support for checksum computation
for UploadPartCopy when the Copy Source does not have or
match the checksum algorithm on the MPU.

The S3 API behavior changes for multipart uploads:

* CreateMultipartUpload accepts x-amz-checksum-algorithm and
  x-amz-checksum-type, persists the selected checksum configuration,
  and returns both values in the response.
* UploadPart validates and persists x-amz-checksum-* values and returns
  the validated checksum in the response. Checksum-aware uploads
  of type COMPOSITE require each part to use the algorithm
  selected at initiation. FULL_OBJECT does not require it.
* UploadPartCopy preserves and returns the source checksum when copying
  the complete source object with a compatible checksum algorithm.
* CompleteMultipartUpload persists and returns the completed checksum
  and checksum type. GetObject and HeadObject return these values when
  x-amz-checksum-mode: ENABLED is requested.
* COMPOSITE checksums support CRC32, CRC32C, SHA1, and SHA256.
  FULL_OBJECT checksums support CRC32, CRC32C, and CRC64NVME.
* FULL_OBJECT checksum usage for MPUs depends on `anycrc` being
  installed in the Swift cluster, if not, a 501 will be thrown on usage attempts.
* UploadPartCopy requests and incompatible source checksums return 501.

See AWS Docs:
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/checking-object-integrity-upload.html

s3api: Checksum Persistence on MPUs

Swift does checksum validation on UploadPart during a
Multi-Part Object Upload, but it does not persist that checksum
metadata after.

Like checksum persistence on full object uploads,
This patch allows users of the s3api to specify a checksum
algorithm during a Multi Part Upload of both
FULL_OBJECT checksum types and also COMPOSITE checksum types.
A user can also just insert specific checksums on UploadPart requests
instead the same checksum on each part the entire MPU lifecycle.

We persist s3api sysmeta headers on the MPU manifest
and use that to decide what checksum algorithm to
enforce in later stages of the MPU lifecycle, and how
to validate the final checksum for the MPU.

During CompleteMultipartUpload, SLO gathers each segment’s
checksum metadata and passes the aligned HEAD response headers
to s3api’s manifest hook. s3api validates the stored part checksums
against any client-provided values, calculates and validates
the completed MPU checksum, and persists the resulting checksum
metadata on the final SLO manifest using the footer callback.

This patch does not add support for checksum computation
for UploadPartCopy.

In the event of mismatched proxy servers versions, we attach a
sysmeta sentinel checksum header, also know as 'checksum-upload-id'
to each MPU part that passes through a new proxy server.
On final checksum computation, any part that does not have the
header, will cause the MPU to be completed without the final
checksum.

The S3 API behavior changes for multipart uploads:

* CreateMultipartUpload accepts x-amz-checksum-algorithm and
  x-amz-checksum-type, persists the selected checksum configuration,
  and returns both values in the response.

* UploadPart validates and persists x-amz-checksum-* values and returns
  the validated checksum in the response. Checksum-aware uploads
  of type COMPOSITE require each part to use the algorithm
  selected at initiation. FULL_OBJECT does not require it.

* CompleteMultipartUpload persists and returns the completed checksum
  and checksum type. GetObject and HeadObject return these values when
  x-amz-checksum-mode: ENABLED is requested.

* COMPOSITE checksums support CRC32, CRC32C, SHA1, and SHA256.

* FULL_OBJECT checksums support CRC32, CRC32C, and CRC64NVME.

* FULL_OBJECT checksum usage for MPUs depends on `anycrc` being
  installed in the Swift cluster, if not, a 501 will be thrown on usage attempts.

See AWS Docs:
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/checking-object-integrity-upload.html

revisions.message:
RBD: server-side copy when uploading a volume to an image

When Glance is backed by the same Ceph cluster as Cinder, uploading a
volume to an image streams the entire volume from Ceph through the
cinder-volume host to the Glance API and back into Ceph. For raw images
this is a pure network round-trip of data that already lives in the
cluster and is prohibitively slow for large volumes.

Add an optional server-side path to RBDDriver.copy_volume_to_image: when
the new ``rbd_glance_pool`` option is set and the image is raw and
uncompressed, snapshot the volume, clone it into the Glance pool,
flatten the clone so it no longer depends on the volume, create the
protected ``snap`` snapshot Glance expects, and register the resulting
RBD location with Glance via the image location API. No image data
crosses the network; the copy is performed entirely within Ceph.

The path is opt-in and only used for raw, uncompressed images sharing
the same Ceph cluster. On any failure the partially created clone and
snapshots are cleaned up and the existing streaming upload is used as a
fallback, so behaviour is unchanged when the option is unset or the
fast path cannot be taken.

Registering the location uses the privileged Glance client, so the
service must be authorized for Glance's add_image_location API
(``[glance]`` credentials with the required role).

Change-Id: Ieefaaefc9fb82aad70c1c6905378641545dae8a2
Signed-off-by: Maximilian Brandt <maximilian.brandt@cloudandheat.com>

revisions.message:
libvirt: Support Cyborg PCI ARQ managed mode

Request Cyborg API microversion 2.4 for ARQ GET requests when the Cyborg
server supports it. Version 2.4 includes the optional managed key in PCI
ARQ attach handle information.

Use that managed key when generating libvirt PCI hostdev XML for Cyborg
ARQs. When managed is false, Nova creates hostdev XML with managed=no so
libvirt does not detach and rebind devices that must remain bound to a
host VFIO variant driver. Missing managed data continues to default to
managed mode for compatibility with older Cyborg services.

Add libvirt functional coverage for managed=false, managed=true, omitted
managed data, and a create/delete lifecycle with managed=false.

Implements: blueprint support-vfio-variant-driver-managed-mode-via-cyborg
Depends-On: https://review.opendev.org/c/openstack/cyborg/+/994575

libvirt: Support Cyborg PCI ARQ managed mode

Request Cyborg API microversion 2.4 for ARQ GET requests when the Cyborg
server supports it. Version 2.4 includes the optional managed key in PCI
ARQ attach handle information. Discover the supported microversion through
the configured keystoneauth adapter so service authentication, TLS, and
retry settings are honored.

Use that managed key when generating libvirt PCI hostdev XML for Cyborg
ARQs. When managed is false, Nova creates hostdev XML with managed=no so
libvirt does not detach and rebind devices that must remain bound to a
host VFIO variant driver. Missing managed data continues to default to
managed mode for compatibility with older Cyborg services. Normalize
boolean and string representations with oslo.utils before generating the
XML value.

Add libvirt functional coverage for managed=false, managed=true, omitted
managed data, and a create/delete lifecycle with managed=false.

revisions.message:
Switch manager pod from bash init.sh to baomon run

Replace the legacy bash init.sh script with baomon run as the manager
pod's main process. This eliminates the bash-based unseal/rekey logic
and uses the Go-based lifecycle manager instead.

Changes in vault-init.yaml statefulset:
- Container args: baomon run --k8s --config /opt/yaml/baomon-config.yaml
- Liveness probe: baomon health <pod> --k8s --config ...
- Removed openbao-init-unseal-3 volume mount (bash script no longer used)
- Added SecretPrefix and GenerationPrefix to baomon ConfigMap

Story: 2011244
Task: 52700

Change-Id: Ie2dac297722b463dd53bf8c59dc22e07b6c2fe99
Signed-off-by: Tae Park <tae.park@windriver.com>

Integrate baomon key shard lifecycle into openbao manager

Replace the bash unseal state machine loop in init.sh with a handoff to
baomon run for perpetual lifecycle management. The init.sh script remains
the container entrypoint because it provides access to helm template
values that baomon cannot read directly from the chart.

The startup flow is: init.sh waits for pods, checks initialization
status, runs first-time init/unseal/raft-join via baomon CLI commands,
removes the health excuse, then execs into baomon run which takes over
as PID 1. baomon run handles perpetual unseal detection, rekey-in-progress
monitoring, and health checks using generation-based immutable secret
storage.

The bash state machine (runStateMachine, PODREC_F, PODREC_TMP_F) is
removed since baomon run provides equivalent functionality with the
new generation-based key shard architecture. The baomon ConfigMap
gains SecretPrefix and GenerationPrefix fields for the generation
secret naming scheme.

Container entrypoint: bash /opt/script/init.sh (unchanged from legacy)
Liveness probe: source init.sh; health_check (bash health function)
Volumes: init script ConfigMap + baomon config ConfigMap + CA cert secret

Test Plan:
PASS  Deploy openbao app on AIO-SX, verify init.sh execs into baomon run
PASS  Verify baomon run detects and unseals sealed servers
PASS  Verify manager pod restart recovers state from K8s

Respect Depends-On for service projects

Historically OpenStack-Ansible was not respecting Depends-On for service
projects. This was related to quite some level of complexity

letsencrypt: Add ACME dns-01 challenge support

So far the letsencrypt role only supported the ACME http-01 challenge,
which requires Horizon, the letsencrypt-webserver container and HAProxy
proxying of /.well-known/acme-challenge.

This adds support for the ACME dns-01 challenge, selected with the new
letsencrypt_challenge variable (default http-01, so existing deployments
are unaffected). The implementation is provider agnostic: any DNS
provider supported by the bundled lego binary can be used by naming it in
letsencrypt_dns_provider and supplying the environment variables it
expects through the generic letsencrypt_lego_dns_environment
mapping.

When the dns-01 challenge is selected, the letsencrypt-webserver
container, the HAProxy acme_client backend and the acme-challenge
redirect exception are skipped, as none of them are needed. Prechecks
validate the challenge type, the DNS provider and the provider
credentials. Extra lego DNS flags can be forwarded through
letsencrypt_lego_dns_additional_opts.

This depends on the kolla change adding dns-01 support to the
letsencrypt-lego image.

Add worst-case Changed Block Tracking (CBT) scenario test

Add a scenario test that stresses the os-list_changed_blocks volume
action -- the first Cinder API that can return a very large payload. The
driver ships the whole changed-extent list from cinder-volume to
cinder-api over RPC, and the API windows it for the HTTP response, so a
large list exercises both the AMQP reply path and HTTP pagination (and
note that HTTP pagination does not relieve the RPC layer, which transfers
the full list on every page).

The test boots a server, attaches a volume, writes many isolated blocks
(each separated by a gap so the backend cannot consolidate them) between
two snapshots, then pages through the changed-block list asserting the
pagination contract holds and the extents are well formed. It also walks
the full allocation map (no base snapshot). It self-skips if the backend
or microversion does not support CBT (HTTP 409/406).

A ChangedBlocksClient service client issues the os-list_changed_blocks
action at microversion 3.72. A new non-voting job,
cinder-tempest-plugin-cbt-lvm-thin, runs the test against a thin LVM
backend, which implements the CBT driver API; it is non-voting during
rollout and self-skips until the CBT framework and thin-LVM CBT driver
land.

Depends-On: https://review.opendev.org/c/openstack/cinder/+/990923
Depends-On: https://review.opendev.org/c/openstack/cinder/+/995738

Change-Id: I8c6d284ceb1b06fef1b441a767f76212d31ef8ed

Add worst-case Changed Block Tracking (CBT) scenario test

Add a scenario test that stresses the os-list_changed_blocks volume
action -- the first Cinder API that can describe a very large number of
changed regions. The offset/length/marker/limit window is pushed all the
way down to the volume driver, so only the requested page is held in
memory and crosses Oslo RPC to cinder-api; this test verifies that path
stays correct and bounded for a large, heavily fragmented volume.

The test boots a server, attaches a volume, writes many isolated blocks
(each separated by a gap so the backend cannot consolidate them) between
two snapshots, then: pages through the changed-block list asserting the
pagination contract holds and the extents are well formed; walks the full
allocation map (no base snapshot); confirms a byte window (offset/length)
restricts the result to the requested range; and checks that paging one
extent at a time is lossless versus the larger-page walk. It self-skips
if the backend or microversion does not support CBT (HTTP 409/406).

A ChangedBlocksClient service client issues the os-list_changed_blocks
action at microversion 3.72. A new non-voting job,
cinder-tempest-plugin-cbt-lvm-thin, runs the test against a thin LVM
backend, which implements the CBT driver API; it is non-voting during
rollout and self-skips until the CBT framework and thin-LVM CBT driver
land.

Add Changed Block Tracking (CBT) scenario tests

Add scenario tests for both consumers of Changed Block Tracking.

The first stresses the os-list_changed_blocks volume action -- the Cinder
API that can describe a very large number of changed regions. The
offset/length/marker/limit window is pushed all the way down to the volume
driver, so only the requested page is held in memory and crosses Oslo RPC
to cinder-api; the test verifies that path stays correct and bounded for a
large, heavily fragmented volume. It boots a server, attaches a volume,
writes many isolated blocks (each separated by a gap so the backend cannot
consolidate them) between two snapshots, then: pages through the
changed-block list asserting the pagination contract holds and the extents
are well formed; walks the full allocation map (no base snapshot); confirms
a byte window restricts the result; and checks that paging one extent at a
time is lossless versus the larger-page walk. It self-skips if the backend
or microversion does not support CBT (HTTP 409/406). A ChangedBlocksClient
service client issues the action at microversion 3.72.

The second exercises the other CBT consumer, cinder-backup, end to end --
the parts only a real backup/restore can cover. It backs up an in-use
volume (so the backup is taken from a temporary snapshot the framework
adopts as the CBT reference point), takes a full then an incremental
backup, and restores both, comparing a whole-device md5 of the source at
backup time against each restored volume. It covers the sparse-full backup
(holes reproduced as zeros), the data->zero incremental case (a region
overwritten with zeros must still be shipped), and -- by restoring the
sparse full over a pre-dirtied existing volume -- the restore-side
zero-fill path. A dropped changed extent or an un-zeroed hole shows up as
an md5 mismatch.

The non-voting cinder-tempest-plugin-cbt-lvm-thin job runs both tests
against a thin LVM backend (which implements the CBT driver API) and now
also configures cinder-backup with the Swift chunked backup driver, since
CBT only engages for the chunked backup drivers. It is non-voting during
rollout and self-skips until the CBT framework and thin-LVM CBT driver
land.

Depends-On: https://review.opendev.org/c/openstack/cinder/+/990923
Depends-On: https://review.opendev.org/c/openstack/cinder/+/995738

Add NVMe/FC transport to the NVMe-oF connector

Add Fibre Channel as a transport for the existing NVMe-oF connector,
selected by connection info with transport_type='fc'. FC portals carry
an "nn-0x<wwnn>:pn-0x<wwpn>" traddr (port unused); attach uses
"nvme connect --transport fc --traddr <target> --host-traddr <hba>",
iterating the local NVMe-capable FC HBAs. Native NVMe multipath (ANA)
assembles the paths, as for RoCE/TCP.

get_connector_properties now also reports host wwpns/wwnns when FC HBAs
are present (reusing the FC connector's WWN discovery) so NVMe/FC targets
can build the fabric zoning map. RoCE/TCP-only hosts are unchanged.

Change-Id: I0215aa3597b702d4ab2f4699c138e6dbb8ca6464
Signed-off-by: Simon Dodsley <simon@purestorage.com>

Add NVMe/FC transport to the NVMe-oF connector

Add Fibre Channel as a transport for the existing NVMe-oF connector,
selected by connection info with transport_type='fc'. FC portals carry
an "nn-0x<wwnn>:pn-0x<wwpn>" traddr (port unused); attach uses
"nvme connect --transport fc --traddr <target> --host-traddr <hba>",
iterating the local NVMe-capable FC HBAs. Native NVMe multipath (ANA)
assembles the paths, as for RoCE/TCP.

When the host has no local NVMe-capable FC HBA to issue an explicit
connect from (for example the nvme_fcloop loopback used in CI), the
kernel autoconnects the FC controller asynchronously once the rport is
discovered. In that case _connect_target would keep the portal's stale
(None) controller name, treat it as missing on every retry, and fail
with VolumeDeviceNotFound even though the device was present. When no
active connection could be made and the target is FC, refresh the
controller names and re-check for a live controller before giving up,
and allow a couple more retries for the autoconnect to complete.

get_connector_properties now also reports host wwpns/wwnns when FC HBAs
are present (reusing the FC connector's WWN discovery) so NVMe/FC targets
can build the fabric zoning map. RoCE/TCP-only hosts are unchanged.

Depends-On: https://review.opendev.org/c/openstack/os-brick/+/997876

revisions.message:
Install the kerbside-proxy wheel into kerbside images.

Kerbside recently split out the proxying element which shovels SPICE
packets around from the python business logic and re-implemented
the high bandwidth proxy component in rust. The proxy is still pip
installable because of a maturin wrapper, and the kerbside package
depends on the kerbside-proxy package correctly.

However, it might be desirable for developers or deployers to be
able to optionally override the kerbside-proxy wheel when building
images. This patch therefore exposes such an override mechanism.

Change-Id: Iaa556368a1d995a6764bd8b47833cc9472b1bb5d
Signed-off-by: Michael Still <mikal@stillhq.com>

Install the kerbside-proxy wheel into kerbside images.

Kerbside recently split out the proxying element which shovels SPICE
packets around from the python business logic and re-implemented
the high bandwidth proxy component in rust. The proxy is still pip
installable because of a maturin wrapper, and the kerbside package
depends on the kerbside-proxy package correctly.

However, it might be desirable for developers or deployers to be
able to optionally override the kerbside-proxy wheel when building
images. This patch therefore exposes such an override mechanism.

etcd: point kube-apiserver at the fixed cluster and keep it correct

The control plane has to reach every member of the cluster, not only
the floating one, so sysinv builds the kube-apiserver --etcd-servers
list from the members that actually exist and applies it without
rebuilding the control plane.

Cluster membership is derived from the cluster itself rather than from
inventory records. Deployment Manager creates controller-1's inventory
record from the deployment config before the machine is installed, so
_get_etcd_cluster_endpoints() now asks etcd directly via
get_cluster_members() rather than relying on a NodeNotFound guard.

The HAProxy backend list is gated on provisioning state: a host
reaches PROVISIONED only once it has been installed and configured.
_get_apiserver_addresses() publishes the provisioned set as
platform::kubernetes::params::apiserver_addresses.

The simplex-to-duplex conversion changes membership, so the conductor
applies the conversion manifest when the system mode changes and
reconciles the endpoint list once the conversion has run.

create-etcd-certs: Add controller unit IPs to etcd certificate SANs

Add cluster-host unit addresses (controller-0, controller-1) to the
subject_alt_name field of etcd-server and apiserver-etcd-client CSRs
generated during bootstrap. This ensures etcd mTLS works on per-controller
addresses when etcd runs as a multi-member cluster.

This prepares the certificates for the Active+Active kube-apiserver
architecture where etcd runs as a 3-member
Raft cluster with fixed members bound to per-controller cluster-host
addresses.

SANs after this change:
- IP: cluster_floating_address (VIP)
- IP: controller_0_cluster_host (unit address)
- IP: controller_1_cluster_host (unit address)
- IP: 127.0.0.1 (loopback)

PASS: Validated on live AIO-DX VLM lab (192.168.206.1/2/3)

- IP: controller_0_cluster_host (unit address)
- IP: controller_1_cluster_host (unit address, DX only)
- IP: 127.0.0.1 (IPv4 loopback)
- IP: ::1 (IPv6 loopback)

Signed-off-by: Bhushan Bhaskar Dhikale <BhushanBhaskar.Dhikale@windriver.com>

ansible: Bootstrap and restore simplex with etcd-fixed

As part of the etcd architecture redesign, the source of truth for the
etcd cluster is moving from the DRBD-backed floating member to the local
disk fixed-0 member on controller-0.

For simplex deployments, the SM-managed floating etcd instance will no
longer exist. This commit updates the Ansible playbooks to also target
the etcd-fixed systemd service when stopping or starting etcd, ensuring
that both standalone (simplex) and floating (duplex) instances are
appropriately handled during bringup and restore operations.

In addition, it sets etcd_endpoint to controller-0 cluster-host
address for simplex since the floating IP is not used for etcd.

etcd: add certificate SANs and update backup/restore for fixed member

Two related pieces of the fixed-bootstraps-first etcd work that share
files, kept together so they do not collide in review.

Certificate SANs. The etcd cluster on duplex and standard systems runs a
fixed member on each controller, bound to that controller's cluster-host
unit address, alongside the floating member. All members share a single
certificate, so it must carry every address a member can be reached on or
the mTLS handshake fails. Extend the SAN list generated at bootstrap from
{floating, IPv4 loopback} to {floating, controller-0 unit, controller-1
unit, IPv4 loopback, IPv6 loopback}, taking the unit addresses from the
facts validate-config already computes. Those collapse to the floating
address on simplex, and unique() then drops the duplicate so a simplex
certificate carries only addresses that exist.

Backup and restore. Back up from the fixed member endpoints rather than
the floating address, and expose the controller-0 fixed address as its own
fact for callers that need a single authoritative endpoint. Restore the
snapshot into the fixed-0 data directory, which becomes the cluster seed;
the floating member is added later, at controller-0 unlock.

The restore must supply cluster membership explicitly. etcd validates that
--name appears in --initial-cluster, and the built-in default
("default=http://localhost:2380") does not contain fixed-0, so without
--initial-cluster, --initial-cluster-token and
--initial-advertise-peer-urls the restore fails outright:

  Error: couldn't find local name "fixed-0" in the initial cluster
  configuration

The token and peer URL are matched to what puppet writes to
/etc/default/etcd-fixed so the member starts against the restored data.
--mark-compacted and --bump-revision are applied on the etcdutl path only;
they were added to etcdutl in etcd 3.5.9 and etcdctl does not accept them.

Also stop etcd-fixed alongside the floating instance when bootstrap tears
services down for a replay. Neither stop may fail the play, since the
floating instance does not exist on simplex and etcd-fixed may be absent
on an older configuration.

PASS: AIO-DX build 2007, etcd 3.6.9 -- both etcd-server and
      apiserver-etcd-client certificates carry all five SANs:
      192.168.206.1, 192.168.206.2, 192.168.206.3, 127.0.0.1, ::1
PASS: simplex SAN list collapses to floating, 127.0.0.1 and ::1
PASS: backup snapshot taken from the fixed member endpoints
      (26 MB, 2124 keys, revision 31299)
PASS: restore into /opt/etcd-fixed/db/fixed-0.etcd succeeds with rc=0;
      etcdutl reports "added member fixed-0", "bumping latest revision
      31299 -> 1000031299" and "marking revision compacted"
PASS: etcd-fixed starts against the restored data directory and a key
      written before the backup reads back unchanged after the restore
PASS: without the membership flags the same restore fails with
      'couldn't find local name "fixed-0" in the initial cluster
      configuration'
PASS: etcd and etcd-fixed both stopped on bootstrap replay
PASS: ansible-playbooks-tox-linters, -pep8, -bandit

The backup addressed the floating cluster-host address, which does not
exist on a simplex -- the endpoint rendered as https://False:2379
because the address key is defined but empty, so the default filter
never fired. The snapshot now walks an ordered list of candidate
endpoints, loopback first, and stops at the first that answers; etcdctl
tolerates endpoints that are down, so the same list serves simplex and
duplex.

Restore replaces the fixed member's database. It has to stop the member
first: the bootstrap manifest has already started etcd-fixed against an
empty data directory, and replacing the files underneath a running member
left the restored database discarded and the cluster holding 302 keys
where the backup had 2608. The member is stopped, its data replaced, and
then started against the restored database rather than merely enabled.

Five additions bring this to the High Level Design, section 9.

Backup addresses the fixed members on their cluster-host unit addresses rather
than the floating address, because the fixed members are the authoritative
local-disk copies and are present on every system type. etcdctl rejects more
than one endpoint for a snapshot on the count alone, before reachability is
considered, so the endpoints are tried one at a time and the first that answers
is used; a partial file from a failed attempt is removed before the next, and
only the failure of every endpoint is fatal. That is what lets a backup succeed
with one fixed member down.

The cluster membership is now recorded alongside the snapshot, each member name
and peer URL in machine-readable form. The restore rebuilds the cluster rather
than restoring it, and compares the recorded topology against the system it is
restoring onto, so that a restore onto a differently sized or differently
addressed system is identified before any member starts.

The restored member's name is read from /etc/default/etcd-fixed rather than
assumed. The environment file and the restore target must name the same
directory: snapshot restore creates whatever directory it is given, so a
mismatch is not reported -- the database ends up somewhere etcd never opens and
the member starts as an empty single-member cluster instead of failing. On
simplex there is no peer to replicate from, so the data would be lost with no
error raised anywhere in the procedure. The two are now compared and a mismatch
fails loudly. fixed-N naming applies only to systems with more than one
controller, so it cannot be assumed here.

The restored member is rendered with ETCD_INITIAL_CLUSTER_STATE=new, the only
use of new outside bootstrap. The restored data carries the membership of the
cluster that was backed up, which no longer exists; left in place the member
starts expecting peers that are gone and waits for a quorum that can never
form.

The restore then verifies the result before any other member rejoins: exactly
one member, and no address belonging to the cluster that was backed up. A
member that came up retaining the prior membership believes in peers that no
longer exist, and there is no recovery short of wiping the data directory and
restoring again, so this is checked while wiping is still cheap.

Addresses are formatted for URL use through a shared pattern that brackets an
IPv6 literal per RFC 2732, leaves IPv4 unchanged, and leaves an already
bracketed literal alone rather than nesting brackets. An unbracketed IPv4
address is a valid host:port, so this defect class is invisible on IPv4 and
fires only on IPv6.

The Bullseye branch had the same defect for the same reason; it was
simply not exercised on a Trixie system. Bracket the addresses with
regex_replace instead, which is a built-in and therefore resolvable
through map(). This also matches the reasoning already recorded on the
restore path, where the filter is avoided because it lives in a
different collection on Bullseye and Trixie, and lets the two
distro-specific tasks collapse into one.

Verified on an AIO-DX system that the formatting is correct for both
address families:
  192.168.206.2,192.168.206.3 -> 192.168.206.2:2379,https://192.168.206.3
  fd01::2,fd01::3             -> [fd01::2]:2379,https://[fd01::3]

Five additions bring this to the High Level Design, section 9.

Backup addresses the fixed members on their cluster-host unit addresses rather
than the floating address, because the fixed members are the authoritative
local-disk copies and are present on every system type. etcdctl rejects more
than one endpoint for a snapshot on the count alone, before reachability is
considered, so the endpoints are tried one at a time and the first that answers
is used; a partial file from a failed attempt is removed before the next, and
only the failure of every endpoint is fatal. That is what lets a backup succeed
with one fixed member down.

The cluster membership is now recorded alongside the snapshot, each member name
and peer URL in machine-readable form. The restore rebuilds the cluster rather
than restoring it, and compares the recorded topology against the system it is
restoring onto, so that a restore onto a differently sized or differently
addressed system is identified before any member starts.

The restored member's name is read from /etc/default/etcd-fixed rather than
assumed. The environment file and the restore target must name the same
directory: snapshot restore creates whatever directory it is given, so a
mismatch is not reported -- the database ends up somewhere etcd never opens and
the member starts as an empty single-member cluster instead of failing. On
simplex there is no peer to replicate from, so the data would be lost with no
error raised anywhere in the procedure. The two are now compared and a mismatch
fails loudly. fixed-N naming applies only to systems with more than one
controller, so it cannot be assumed here.

The restored member is rendered with ETCD_INITIAL_CLUSTER_STATE=new, the only
use of new outside bootstrap. The restored data carries the membership of the
cluster that was backed up, which no longer exists; left in place the member
starts expecting peers that are gone and waits for a quorum that can never
form.

The restore then verifies the result before any other member rejoins: exactly
one member, and no address belonging to the cluster that was backed up. A
member that came up retaining the prior membership believes in peers that no
longer exist, and there is no recovery short of wiping the data directory and
restoring again, so this is checked while wiping is still cheap.

Addresses are formatted for URL use through a shared pattern that brackets an
IPv6 literal per RFC 2732, leaves IPv4 unchanged, and leaves an already
bracketed literal alone rather than nesting brackets. An unbracketed IPv4
address is a valid host:port, so this defect class is invisible on IPv4 and
fires only on IPv6.

The snapshot is taken from one endpoint. etcdctl rejects a list here on
the count alone, before reachability is considered -- "snapshot must be
requested to one selected node, not multiple" -- so passing both fixed
addresses fails on every system type. etcd_endpoint is left as it is for
the calls that do accept a list.

The endpoint also has to survive a system with no per-controller
addresses. On AIO-SX the cluster-host pool defines only a floating
address; controller-0's cluster-host address is that address, and
controller0_address comes back false. A Jinja default() does not cover
this because the value is defined and falsy rather than undefined, so it
never fires and the endpoint renders as the literal string "False". On a
simplex lab that produced:

  etcdctl --endpoints https://False:2379,https://False:2379 snapshot save
  Error: snapshot must be requested to one selected node, not multiple

with the backup failing and no archive written. The fixed endpoint now
falls back to the floating address, which is the same address the fixed
member binds on that system type.

Drop the ETCDCTL_API environment block. etcd 3.6 no longer reads it and
logs "unrecognized environment variable" on every invocation.

Test-Plan: WRCPPV-11147

The etcd membership record is now actually archived. It was generated and
guarded by a hard failure task, but omitted from final_backup_targets, so tar
never picked it up and the file was discarded with the ansible temp directory.
A stock backup produced a tarball containing only etcd-snapshot.db and
etcd-binary-version; with the file listed the tarball carries
etcd-members.json recording every member. Reproduced on both duplex and
simplex, so the omission was topology-independent.

The surrounding comments claimed the restore compares the recorded topology
against the system being restored onto. It does not. The record is archived
for forensics -- what the cluster looked like at backup time, which a support
bundle otherwise cannot answer. A useful comparison would have to be against
the target's configured topology, since a duplex backup records three members
while the restore target is a freshly installed controller-0 with exactly one;
a recorded-versus-live check would reject every valid duplex restore. That is
left as follow-up rather than shipped half-understood, and the comments now say
so.

sysinv: Add controller unit IPs to etcd certificate SANs on renewal

This is a follow-up to the review "create-etcd-certs: Add controller
unit IPs to etcd certificate SANs" [1], which adds the SANs during
bootstrap. This commit handles the certificate renewal path.

Add resolution of cluster-host unit addresses from /etc/hosts for etcd
certificate renewal. Puppet (via sysinv/puppet/platform.py) populates
/etc/hosts with controller-X-cluster-host entries on both controllers,
making this approach reliable on both active and standby without any
DRBD/PostgreSQL dependency.

The renewed apiserver-etcd-client and etcd-server certificates now
include SANs for the floating IP, both controller unit IPs, IPv4
loopback, and IPv6 loopback.

Changes:
- get_cluster_host_unit_ip(): resolves unit address by parsing
  /etc/hosts via awk. Falls back to floating+N arithmetic if entry
  is missing.
- SANs: IP.1=floating, IP.2=ctrl-0, IP.3=ctrl-1, IP.4=127.0.0.1,
  IP.5=::1
- Works identically on active and standby controllers (no DB needed)
- IPv4 and IPv6 compatible

Story: 2010302
Task: 51206

Depends-On: If43551474a35f26d95d11a53fb028880faf4f230
Change-Id: Ia1f14bf0058e126bf00802be507cd34b809f6d1a
Signed-off-by: Bhushan Bhaskar Dhikale <BhushanBhaskar.Dhikale@windriver.com>

sysinv: add controller unit IPs to etcd certificate SANs on renewal

This is the renewal counterpart to the bootstrap change "etcd: add
certificate SANs and update backup/restore for fixed member". Bootstrap
generates the etcd certificates with SANs for the floating address, both
controller cluster-host unit addresses and the loopbacks;
kube-cert-rotation.sh must regenerate them with the same set, or the fixed
etcd members become unreachable over mTLS after the first renewal.

Resolve the cluster-host unit addresses by parsing /etc/hosts, where puppet
(via sysinv/puppet/platform.py) writes a controller-X-cluster-host entry on
both controllers. This works identically on the active and the standby
controller, with no dependency on DRBD or PostgreSQL, which matters because
renewal can run on either. If an entry is missing, fall back to deriving the
address from the floating address and log a warning.

The renewed apiserver-etcd-client and etcd-server certificates then carry
IP.1=floating, IP.2=controller-0 unit, IP.3=controller-1 unit,
IP.4=127.0.0.1 and IP.5=::1 -- the same set bootstrap produces.

Test Plan:

      SANs (192.168.206.1, 192.168.206.2, 192.168.206.3, 127.0.0.1, ::1)
      on both etcd-server and apiserver-etcd-client; the renewal SAN set
      matches
PASS: unit addresses resolved from /etc/hosts on the active controller
PASS: fallback derivation produces the correct addresses when an entry is
      absent
PASS: etcd accepts the renewed certificate without service disruption

Fix TLS leaf certificate renewal fallback

Migrate sunbeam TLS requirers from the deprecated tls-certificates
interface library to charmlibs.interfaces.tls_certificates and wire
update-status as a refresh event.

This gives charms a periodic renewal safety net when secret-expired does
not complete, preventing leaf certificates from remaining expired until
workloads fail after restart.

Fix TLS leaf certificate renewal fallback

Migrate sunbeam TLS requirers from the deprecated tls-certificates
interface library to charmlibs.interfaces.tls_certificates and wire
update-status as a refresh event.

This gives charms a periodic renewal safety net when secret-expired does
not complete, preventing leaf certificates from remaining expired until
workloads fail after restart.

The refresh may emit certificate-available events when the certificate
material has not changed. Persist certificate bundle fingerprints and
skip duplicate events to avoid unnecessary charm reconciliation and
workload service restarts.

Only record a fingerprint after configure_charm completes successfully,
so failures handled by the charm guard remain eligible for retry. Prevent
synchronous certificate callbacks from re-entering reconciliation while
certificates are being synchronized.

Closes-Bug: #2159609
Depends-On: https://review.opendev.org/c/openstack/sunbeam-charms/+/1000804

Add puppet exec to clear federation deferred flag

Change-Id: Ieac8ef3722e6300026473d0ec219da0c46d6dc8f
Signed-off-by: Felipe Vasconcelos <Felipe.Vasconcelos@windriver.com>

Add puppet exec to clear federation deferred flag

After the keystone federation class applies (or cleans up) resources,
remove the .federation_config_required flag file. This ensures the
conductor periodic audit does not re-trigger puppet on the next cycle.

Placing the removal in puppet (rather than sysinv) provides natural
retry: if puppet fails at any earlier step, the flag remains and the
conductor retries on the next audit interval (~60s).

The exec is added to both the 'if $oidc_issuer_url' branch (after
resource creation) and the 'else' branch (after resource cleanup)
in both bullseye and trixie subtrees.

Test plan:
PASS: Upgrade 26.03 to 26.09, verify flag removed after puppet applies
federation resources (conductor log shows single trigger, no repeated
attempts).
PASS: Simulate puppet failure (e.g. keystone unresponsive), verify flag
persists and conductor retries on next cycle.
PASS: Fresh install, verify flag created by manifest/post and removed
after puppet runs via operation/post path.

Depends-On: https://review.opendev.org/c/starlingx/config/+/995395

revisions.message:
Add the track attributions API

Lets a subject see and govern who they are recorded as having been
aboard with, and gives vehicle managers the manual escape hatch.

The authorization split is the point of the whole design, so it is
narrow on purpose.  A subject sets the public flag on their own
association and nobody else's -- not even the vehicle's owner, who
governs the track's visibility instead.  A manager who wants a track
private changes the track, not someone else's association with it.

A coalesced group association is not directly settable at all: its
value is the conjunction of its members' own choices, so allowing it to
be set would let one member publish another's presence.  That returns a
409 explaining it is derived.

Changing a flag re-resolves the track, because a coalesced group's
derived value depends on its members' effective values and would
otherwise sit stale until something else touched the vehicle.

Manual attributions cover "the resolver missed it" or "the guest never
checked in", and only vehicle managers can add or remove them.  Removal
is refused for resolver-owned rows: those are derived facts, withdrawn
by the resolver when their check-ins stop overlapping, not by hand.

aboard with, and gives vehicle managers the manual escape hatch.

narrow on purpose.  A subject sets the public flag on their own

upsert() loops now instead of trusting the row it read.  It decides
from a snapshot and then writes by id, and withdraw_manual() deletes a
manual-only record outright: a withdrawal landing in that window left
the conditional update matching nothing, and returning None there
threw away the automatic support the resolver had just computed -- the
association would disappear from the subject's map until some later
run happened to recreate it.  A vanished row now sends it back for a
fresh read, where it inserts instead; a concurrent insert of the same
(track_id, subject_id) pair is caught on the unique index and folded
into the winner the same way.  This is the pattern withdraw_manual
already uses, and the write half is split into _write_upsert() so the
retry reads as one decision per attempt.

revisions.message:
Raise DRBD cpu-mask limit from 112 to 908 CPUs

The DRBD cpu-mask was limited to 112 CPUs (28 hex chars) due to a
32-byte buffer in drbdsetup. Upstream drbd-utils commit e404ad9
increased this buffer to 256 bytes, supporting up to 908 CPUs.

This change updates sysinv to match the new upstream limit:
- cpu_utils.py: raise DRBD_CPU_MASK_LIMIT from 112 to 908
- puppet/platform.py: raise mask truncation from 28 to 227 hex chars

This change requires the corresponding cherry-pick of upstream
drbd-utils commit e404ad9 into StarlingX's drbd-utils package.

Closes-Bug: 2162016

Test Plan:
TODO: host-cpu-modify accepts platform cores with id > 112 and < 908
TODO: host-cpu-modify rejects platform cores with id >= 908
TODO: AIO install with >112-core system, mixed function - DRBD comes up
TODO: AIO install with <112-core system - no regression

instance on controller-0 founds the cluster and additional members

sysinv: Add etcd cluster membership helper functions

Add helper functions to sysinv/common/etcd.py for managing etcd
cluster membership in the multi-instance topology, where the fixed
instance on controller-0 founds the cluster and additional members
(the DRBD-backed floating instance, and the fixed instance on
controller-1) join the running cluster.

Functions added:
- get_members(): list cluster members with raw etcdctl JSON fields
- member_exists(): check membership by name
- add_member(): idempotent 'etcdctl member add', returns member ID
- remove_member(): idempotent 'etcdctl member remove' by name
- is_endpoint_healthy() / wait_for_endpoint(): endpoint health polling
- get_configured_member_count(): expected size for the system mode
- is_voting_member(): whether a member counts towards quorum
- get_cluster_health(): healthy/total counts and degraded member names

Cluster health is accounted for as the high level design requires.
Two points follow from that design and are reflected here:

- Health is measured against the member count the system is
  configured for, not the count currently registered. The two differ
  only while a procedure is deliberately growing or shrinking the
  cluster, and an alarm keyed to the registered count would assert
  continuously through those steps and gate the very operations it
  exists to protect. get_cluster_health() therefore accepts the
  system mode and reports missing members explicitly. The parameter
  is optional, so existing callers keep the previous behaviour.

- A learner is never counted healthy. It replicates the log but does
  not vote, so it cannot keep the cluster available, and etcd refuses
  the health RPC against it in any case. Such a member is reported as
  "<name> (learner)" to distinguish a member that needs promoting
  from one that needs recovering.

These are consumed by the conductor for cluster lifecycle operations
(simplex-to-duplex migration, platform upgrade and rollback) and by
the periodic cluster health audit.

Unit tests cover the configured member count per system mode, voter
and learner classification, and the health accounting for a fully
healthy cluster, a learner member, an unregistered member, an
unreachable member, a member without a client URL, simplex, an empty
member list, and the no-system-mode fallback.

Test-Plan: WRCPPV-11147

Signed-off-by: bhushan.dhikale <BhushanBhaskar.Dhikale@windriver.com>

sysinv: Add etcd cluster health helpers, audit alarm and upgrade gate

Introduce the etcd cluster health surface used across the
Active+Active control plane work:

* sysinv/common/etcd.py — membership and health helpers
  (get_members, member_exists, add_member, remove_member,
  is_endpoint_healthy, wait_for_endpoint, get_cluster_health)
  with unit coverage.
* conductor/manager.py — periodic _audit_etcd_cluster_health task
  raising the management-affecting 850.003 alarm when the cluster
  is short of its configured member count, clearing once every
  member is a healthy voter again. Audit interval defaults to 60s
  to satisfy the 60-second alarm requirement. Skipped on simplex.
* common/health.py — pre-upgrade gate refusing to start a platform
  upgrade while the etcd cluster is degraded, with unit coverage.

The helpers, the audit and the gate share the same health
evaluation, so they are delivered together; splitting them left
the gate and the audit each depending on an unreviewable subset
of the helpers.

The 850.003 alarm definition is registered separately in
starlingx/fault.

Depends-On: https://review.opendev.org/c/starlingx/fault/+/998292

The cluster health query no longer depends on the local member. It
previously used only the loopback endpoint, so when the local member was
the one that had failed the member list came back empty and the audit
reported nothing healthy and named no failed member:

  850.003  etcd cluster degraded: 0/3 healthy voting members (degraded: )

observed on a duplex system where two of the three members were in fact
healthy and serving. That is the least useful answer at exactly the
moment it matters most, and it would send an operator looking for a
cluster-wide outage that had not happened.

The query now names every member cluster-host endpoint. etcdctl accepts
a list for a member list and tolerates entries that do not answer, so the
audit sees the cluster through whichever members remain. Names that do
not resolve are skipped, which keeps the list correct on simplex, where
the floating and controller-0 names resolve to the same address, and
during the window before a controller has been provisioned.

observed on a duplex system where two of the three members were in fact

The query now names every member cluster-host endpoint. etcdctl accepts

Adds ensure_cert_sans(), which regenerates the etcd certificates when
they do not name every member address. A system upgraded from a release
that ran a single DRBD-backed instance carries a certificate whose SANs
name only the floating address and the loopback addresses:

  SAN: IP Address:192.168.206.1, IP Address:127.0.0.1

The fixed instances bind the controller cluster-host addresses, so every
TLS connection to them fails verification:

  x509: certificate is valid for 192.168.206.1, 127.0.0.1,
        not 192.168.206.2

which surfaces as the member never becoming healthy and so never being
promoted, leaving the cluster short of its members with no indication
that a certificate is the cause.

The regenerated certificate is a union with what is already present
rather than a replacement, so the floating address is never dropped --
the caller names the fixed members, and the floating instance is the one
member serving the cluster while the others are being added.

The CA, validity and extension set match kube-cert-rotation.sh, so a
certificate produced here and one produced by the next scheduled rotation
are equivalent. Nothing is done when every address is already covered,
which makes this safe to call on every activate and a no-op on simplex,
where controller-0 cluster-host address and the floating address are the
same and so already present.

Tests cover reaching the cluster with nothing on loopback, honouring an
explicit endpoint, never emitting a hostname endpoint, simplex deduplication,

healthy and serving. That is the least useful answer at exactly the

cluster-wide outage that had not happened.

Addresses are deduplicated, since on simplex the floating and controller-0
names resolve to the same address and listing it twice would weigh one member

been registered but has not yet started carries no name -- etcd only learns

default, a name-only check reported every freshly added member as absent. The
caller then concluded the add had not taken, either adding it again -- which
etcd rejects for the duplicate peer URL -- or treating the add as failed and
never starting the member.

general answer.

nothing.
