sysinv: add etcd membership and health helpers

Add the helpers the conductor needs to inspect and change etcd cluster
membership, and an audit that alarms when the cluster is degraded.

common/etcd.py gains membership operations (list, add, promote, remove,
find) and health operations (per-endpoint health, wait-for-endpoint,
whole-cluster health). Three properties of etcd shape the interface:

  - A member is identified by peer URL as well as by name, because etcd
    assigns a name only when the member starts and introduces itself. A
    member registered but not yet started carries an empty name, so a
    name-only lookup reports it absent.

  - Members are registered as learners. Registration changes the quorum
    requirement at the moment it happens rather than when the member
    starts, so registering a voter into a cluster of N voters requires
    (N+1)/2+1 while only N are running. On the smallest clusters that is
    immediately fatal.

  - Endpoints are addresses, not names. The etcd certificates carry IP
    subjectAltNames and no DNS names, so a hostname endpoint fails
    verification against every member.

Endpoints are resolved from the cluster-host names rather than assuming
loopback. Loopback is served by the fixed instance; the floating instance
listens only on the cluster-host floating address, so during an upgrade
activate, when the fixed instances are deliberately not started, nothing
answers on it.

Every etcdctl invocation is bounded by a timeout. These calls otherwise
hang rather than fail, waiting on TLS handshake, name resolution, leader
election and request forwarding, and a hung call in the periodic audit
holds the conductor greenthread for its duration.

health.py reports etcd in the base system health query, so a degraded
cluster is visible to any caller rather than only on the platform upgrade
path. The Kubernetes version upgrade and root CA update paths opt out:
neither changes etcd membership, and gating a root CA update on etcd
health would block the operation needed to recover from an etcd
certificate that no longer matches the cluster.

The conductor audits cluster health periodically and raises alarm 850.003
when the cluster is short of its configured member count, clearing it once
every member is a healthy voter again. Health is measured against the
configured topology rather than the registered membership, so the alarm
does not assert continuously while a procedure is deliberately growing or
shrinking the cluster.

Add the helpers the conductor uses to read and change etcd cluster
membership, and report cluster health from a periodic audit that raises
alarm 850.003 when the cluster is short of its configured member count.

Every etcdctl invocation carries etcdctl's own --command-timeout and
--dial-timeout rather than only a wall-clock bound on the subprocess, so
a call is cut short where it can actually be interrupted. Defaults are
5s command and 2s dial, matching the duplex migration script so the two
sources stay aligned; membership changes use 15s because they commit
through raft, and a snapshot save 30s because it streams the keyspace.
The subprocess bound is derived as dial + command + 1s so the two cannot
drift.

Health is measured against the configured topology rather than the
registered membership, so the alarm does not assert continuously while a
procedure is deliberately growing or shrinking the cluster.

collect: add NUMA topology info to collect_extra

Adds numa.info with the following commands:
- numactl --hardware : NUMA node memory totals and distances
- numastat -m        : per-node free/used memory breakdown
- lstopo ASCII       : per-node topology in text form

Adds the following SVG files to var/extra/:

  numa_topology.svg
    Full-system topology showing all NUMA nodes, CPU sockets,
    cores, threads, L1/L2/L3 caches and memory per node.

  numa_topology_node<N>.svg
    Per-node topology restricted to node N. One file per node
    found under /sys/devices/system/node/. Useful for comparing
    node layouts on asymmetric topologies such as SNC on Intel
    or NPS2/NPS4 on AMD EPYC.

  SVG files can be opened in any web browser.

revisions.message:
Refactor snapshot functions to use baomon commands

Replace shell logic in snapshot functions with direct baomon command
invocations. This eliminates duplicated logic and aligns with the
generation-based immutable secret storage model.

Changes:
- snapshotPreCheck: Use baomon snapshot precheck with kubectl pod discovery
  (getOpenbaoPods) instead of globalConfig.ServerAddresses for accurate data
- snapshotCreate: Already delegating to baomon; keep as-is
- snapshotSetSecret: Remove (logic now handled by baomon internally)
- snapshotRestore: Simplify to delegate to baomon snapshot restore;
  remove legacy cluster-key-* secret manipulation

Remove legacy helper functions (verified unused after snapshot functions removed):
- reconstructInitResponse: Only called by validateSecrets and snapshotSetSecret
- validateSecrets: Only called by snapshotSetSecret and snapshotRestore
- storeOpenbaoInitSecrets: Only called by snapshotRestore
- deleteShardSecrets: Only called by snapshotRestore
- splitShard: Only called by storeOpenbaoInitSecrets
- mergeKeyJson: Only called by reconstructInitResponse

Rationale:
These functions relied on legacy cluster-key-* mutable secret pattern where
unseal keys were split across 5 separate k8s secrets. With generation-based
immutable secrets (openbao-unseal-gen-001), baomon handles all operations
internally: metadata creation, validation, restoration, and tamper detection
via SHA-256 hashing.

The generation model eliminates the complexity of:
- Reconstructing init responses from split secrets
- Managing mutable secrets that could be partially updated
- Manual hash validation and cleanup

Test Plan:
- PASS    snapshotPreCheck validates all servers unsealed via baomon
- PASS    snapshotCreate delegates to baomon snapshot create command
- PASS    snapshotRestore delegates to baomon snapshot restore command
- PASS    Generation metadata stored as immutable k8s secrets
- PASS    Tamper detection via SHA-256 hash validation works correctly
- PASS    No cluster-key-* secret references remain in code

invocations. This eliminates duplicated logic and aligns with the
generation-based immutable secret storage model.

Changes:

  (getOpenbaoPods) instead of globalConfig.ServerAddresses for accurate data
- snapshotCreate: Already delegating to baomon; keep as-is
- snapshotSetSecret: Remove (logic now handled by baomon internally)
- snapshotRestore: Simplify to delegate to baomon snapshot restore;
  remove legacy cluster-key-* secret manipulation

Remove legacy helper functions (verified unused after snapshot functions removed):
- reconstructInitResponse: Only called by validateSecrets and snapshotSetSecret
- validateSecrets: Only called by snapshotSetSecret and snapshotRestore
- storeOpenbaoInitSecrets: Only called by snapshotRestore
- deleteShardSecrets: Only called by snapshotRestore
- splitShard: Only called by storeOpenbaoInitSecrets
- mergeKeyJson: Only called by reconstructInitResponse

internally: metadata creation, validation, restoration, and tamper detection
via SHA-256 hashing.

- Reconstructing init responses from split secrets
- Managing mutable secrets that could be partially updated
- Manual hash validation and cleanup

via memmap= boot parameter for NVMe BAR0, with GRUB update and reboot.

Add NVMe driver devstack plugin support

Introduce PCI_SIM_DEVICES so a stack can describe PF ownership and
personality explicitly instead of relying on the legacy even/odd PF
split.

The devstack wiring now falls into four pieces:
- topology parsing: parse service:personality entries, derive PF count,
  and re-parse on demand because DevStack re-sources lib/pci_sim across
  phases
- host bring-up: pass NVMe module args only when an NVMe PF is present
  and pre-arm cyborg:nvme VFs with driver_override so the host nvme
  driver stays active until VFIO handoff
- service wiring: reuse topology-aware VF selection for Nova
  alias/device_spec generation and for Cyborg PCI whitelist and NVMe
  driver config
- test fixtures: build UART and NVMe device profiles from the correct
  VF subset so mixed Cyborg topologies create matching resources

Auto-wire nvme_driver when PCI_SIM_DEVICES includes cyborg:nvme, keep
pci_driver limited to cyborg:uart, and propagate the same topology to
Tempest and the local.conf/devstack documentation updates.

not explicitly specified.

sysinv: reconcile etcd cluster membership from an audit

The etcd cluster lifecycle operations added previously had no caller, so
the fixed members were never added during a deploy, never removed during
a rollback, and a simplex-to-duplex conversion never grew the cluster to
include the floating member.

Wire them up from a periodic audit rather than from a single event hook.
Each operation has to wait for the cluster to be reachable before it can
succeed, and that moment does not coincide with any one event: after a
conversion the floating instance can only be added once the seed is
serving, and during a deploy the fixed instances can only join once both
controllers run the new release. Driving this from an audit also means a
conversion or deploy that is interrupted is retried instead of leaving
the cluster short a member.

The audit dispatches on the deploy state and does nothing on any state it
does not recognise, so it stays clear of a deploy that is still moving:

  activate, activate-done                  add the fixed members
  activate-rollback, activate-rollback-done remove the fixed members
  no deploy in progress                    finish a simplex-to-duplex
                                           conversion, marker-guarded

Membership is left alone until the initial configuration is complete, and
while a backup or restore is running, because both relocate the etcd data
directories underneath the running cluster. The rollback path first checks
whether a fixed member is still registered, so a completed rollback does
not repeat the removal on every pass. Failures are logged and retried on
the next pass instead of propagating, and the existing cluster health
audit raises 850.003 if the cluster stays degraded.

Simplex runs a single fixed member and is skipped.

Test plan:
  PASS  flake8 clean at the enforced 120 column limit
  PASS  dispatch routes correctly for every deploy state, including the
        failed and pending states that must be left alone
  PASS  AIO-DX: floating member added after a simplex-to-duplex
        conversion, marker written, second pass is a no-op
  PASS  AIO-DX: fixed members added on deploy activate
  PASS  AIO-DX: fixed members removed on deploy activate-rollback
  PASS  audit is a no-op while a backup or restore is in progress

serving, and during a deploy the fixed instances can only join once both
controllers run the new release. Driving this from an audit also means a
conversion or deploy that is interrupted is retried instead of leaving
the cluster short a member.

The design describes the conversion as triggered by the migration runtime
manifest when the system mode is set. That trigger on its own is not
sufficient here, because the manifest applies before the cluster is
necessarily reachable and an interrupted conversion would leave the
cluster short a member with nothing to retry it. The audit is idempotent
and acts only on recognised deploy states, so it complements that trigger
rather than replacing it.

The audit dispatches on the deploy state and does nothing on any state it

                                           conversion, marker-guarded

directories underneath the running cluster. The rollback path first checks
whether a fixed member is still registered, so a completed rollback does
not repeat the removal on every pass. Failures are logged and retried on

changing. The health audit reports against the configured member count,
so through a deploy activate, a rollback or a conversion the registered
membership is by design below the configured membership and the alarm

controller, so leaving it to fire would block the very procedure that is
driving the change. Those windows are governed by the sequencing and the
explicit health checks inside the procedures themselves. The same
suppression covers a backup or restore, and the period before the initial
configuration completes.

  PASS  AIO-DX: fixed members added on deploy activate
  PASS  AIO-DX: fixed members removed on deploy activate-rollback
  PASS  audit is a no-op while a backup or restore is in progress

Story: 2010302
Task: 51206

_reconcile_etcd_rollback() matches members on peer URL as well as name.

etcd assigns a name only when a member starts and introduces itself, so a
member that was registered but never started lists with an empty name and its
peer URL alone identifying it. Matching on name alone made the remaining list
come back empty, _reconcile_etcd_rollback() returned without doing anything,
and activate-rollback completed having removed nothing -- leaving a stale
member registered against the cluster. Observed on duplex lab unr2603dx during
a 26.03.100 to 26.10 upgrade on build 631.

The peer URL is built the same way add_fixed_etcd_members_for_upgrade() builds
it, through cutils.format_url_address() so IPv6 addresses are bracketed.

Two supporting changes were needed for this to have any effect, and are in the
changes that own those functions: remove_member() now accepts a peer URL and
looks the member up through find_member(), and
remove_fixed_etcd_members_for_rollback() passes it. Without those, detecting
the nameless member would have been followed by a removal that could not act
on it.

Test Plan:
  PASS  a member present only by peer URL is detected and the removal is
        invoked; both controller peer URLs are offered to the lookup.
  PASS  once no member remains the audit does not remove again, so repeated
        passes after a completed rollback are no-ops.
  PASS  IPv6 addresses are bracketed in the peer URL.
  PASS  pycodestyle count on test_manager.py unchanged at 345 and on
        manager.py at 338, all pre-existing.

Signed-off-by: bhushan.dhikale <BhushanBhaskar.Dhikale@windriver.com>

sysinv: reconcile etcd membership from an audit

Drive etcd membership changes from a periodic audit keyed on USM deploy
state, rather than from a single event hook.

An upgrade changes cluster membership at activate and unwinds it at
activate-rollback. Both are long operations that can be retried, and
neither offers a single point at which the work is guaranteed to succeed,
so the reconciliation is expressed as a desired end state that the audit
converges on:

  activate, activate-done              add the fixed members
  activate-rollback, rollback-done     remove them and disable the units
  no deploy in progress                migrate simplex to duplex

Removal and unit disable are a pair. A removed member whose service is
still running cannot rejoin the cluster it was removed from and logs
failed peer requests indefinitely; on the next boot it would start against
a data directory describing a cluster it no longer belongs to.

Members are matched on peer URL as well as name, because a member
registered but never started carries no name. Matched on name alone the
rollback found nothing to remove and completed while leaving a stale
member registered.

cluster is legitimately mid-resize in those states, and asserting there

revisions.message:
Delegate STX-O backup and restore to application

The STX-O backup and restore logic lives in the platform ansible
repository. Application-level changes require a platform change to
follow, which has produced defects where the platform playbooks drifted
from the application (e.g. Bug 2152622, Bug 2153526).

Add a delegation check to restore_openstack.yml and to the OpenStack
section of the backup-system role. When the application ships its own
playbooks at /opt/platform/ansible/<release>/<app-name>/current/
backup-restore/, delegate to them via include_tasks. Otherwise the
existing inline logic runs unchanged as a fallback.

include_tasks is used instead of import_tasks because import_tasks
resolves the file path at parse time, before the when condition is
evaluated. With no application playbook deployed, parse-time resolution
would fail and the fallback would never be reachable.

Restore side: the delegation check needs software_version, which is
produced by backup-restore/prepare-env. That role was previously only
reached through restore-openstack/prepare-env, which runs too late and
is skipped on the continuation pass. Import common/prepare-env and
backup-restore/prepare-env as pre_tasks so host connectivity and
platform context are available before the check. Both are idempotent.

Backup side: the staging directories (mariadb_dir, helm_overrides)
are created by the platform playbook before the delegation check so
the paths are known whichever side writes the dumps. Detecting whether
the application is present also stays with the platform, since it gates
the archive size estimation, tarball creation and transfer.

Also remove helm_overrides_sqldump_dir from the platform tarball target
list (final_backup_targets). That entry was dead code: the STX-O
restore extracts all artifacts from the STX-O tarball exclusively, the
companion mariadb_dir was never in the platform targets, and the
helm_overrides table is already captured by the sysinv pg_dump which
the platform restore replays in full.

Backward compatible: an application that does not ship playbooks keeps
using the inline logic. Forward compatible: an older platform release
ignores the deployed playbooks.

Test Plan:
[PASS] ansible-playbook --syntax-check on restore_openstack.yml
       and backup.yml
[PASS] ansible-playbook --list-tasks confirms common/prepare-env
       and backup-restore/prepare-env run before the delegation check
[PASS] Verified single producer for mariadb_dir and
       helm_overrides_sqldump_dir (no skipped-register clobber)
[PASS] Verified no task under restore-platform or optimized-restore
       extracts helm_overrides*.sql from the platform tarball
[PASS] Delegation and fallback branches validated in local sandbox

STX-O backup (application playbooks absent):
[TODO] Backup with STX-O applied, confirm STX-O tarball has mariadb
       dumps and helm_overrides_dump.sql
[TODO] Backup with STX-O uploaded only, confirm tarball produced
[TODO] Confirm platform tarball no longer contains
       helm_overrides_dump.sql

STX-O backup (application playbooks present):
[TODO] Confirm application playbook is invoked, inline tasks skipped
[TODO] Confirm STX-O tarball contents match the fallback run
[TODO] Confirm OpenStack archive size estimation still runs

STX-O restore (application playbooks absent):
[TODO] Run restore_openstack.yml, confirm inline roles execute
[TODO] Confirm application reaches applied state
[TODO] Confirm continuation pass (restore_openstack_continue) works

STX-O restore (application playbooks present):
[TODO] Confirm application playbook is invoked, inline roles skipped
[TODO] Confirm platform vars visible in delegated playbook
[TODO] Confirm continuation pass takes the same branch

Cross-cutting:

[TODO] DC subcloud backup, confirm both tarballs transferred
[TODO] Old platform + new app tarball: playbooks ignored, B&R works

Add a delegation check to restore_openstack.yml and to the OpenStack

resolves the file path at parse time, before the when condition is
evaluated. With no application playbook deployed, parse-time resolution
would fail and the fallback would never be reachable.

Restore side: the delegation check needs software_version, which is
produced by backup-restore/prepare-env. That role was previously only
reached through restore-openstack/prepare-env, which runs too late and
is skipped on the continuation pass. Import common/prepare-env and
backup-restore/prepare-env as pre_tasks so host connectivity and
platform context are available before the check. Both are idempotent.

Backup side: the staging directories (mariadb_dir, helm_overrides) are
created by the platform playbook before the delegation check so the
paths are known whichever side writes the dumps. Detecting whether the
application is present also stays with the platform, since it gates the
archive size estimation, tarball creation and transfer.

Also remove helm_overrides_sqldump_dir from the platform tarball target
list (final_backup_targets). That entry was dead code: the STX-O restore
extracts all artifacts from the STX-O tarball exclusively, the companion
mariadb_dir was never in the platform targets, and the helm_overrides
table is already captured by the sysinv pg_dump which the platform
restore replays in full.

Backward compatible: an application that does not ship playbooks keeps
using the inline logic. Forward compatible: an older platform release
ignores the deployed playbooks.

revisions.message:
Scale DaemonSet rollouts and restore accurate apply status

Every DaemonSet-bearing chart in the application pins
max_unavailable: 1, so a rolling update replaces pods one node at a
time and rollout duration grows linearly with the number of
openstack-labelled compute nodes. On a 102-node system this puts
several charts far beyond the 30m timeout set on each HelmRelease:
openvswitch takes roughly 3.5 hours and libvirt roughly 2.5 at
measured per-pod cycle times, and nova-compute needs about 44 minutes
on its largest host group. Raising the timeout only relocates the
wall, because the duration stays proportional to node count.

That timeout failure was previously avoided by setting
disableWait: true on the affected releases, which introduced a second
and worse problem. Flux reports such a release Ready as soon as the
manifests are accepted, before any pod has been replaced. Because
sysinv treats the HelmRelease Ready condition as its source of truth,
the application is reported applied and the apply-in-progress alarm is
cleared while pods are still cycling. The documented verification step
of checking that HelmReleases report READY=True passes in that state,
so it does not detect an incomplete rollout. The semantic checks that
reject host-unlock and host-swact during an apply are released at the
same moment, so those operations are accepted while replacements are
still in flight. A pod that fails to start or crash-loops during the
rollout is not surfaced as a release failure, because nothing is
waiting on readiness.

Fix both together, since the second cannot be fixed without the
first.

Express max_unavailable as 10% on libvirt, openvswitch, ceilometer,
nova and pci-irq-affinity-agent. Kubernetes resolves a DaemonSet
maxUnavailable percentage by rounding up against
status.desiredNumberScheduled, so the wave count becomes ceil(1/p)
and is independent of node count: any of these charts completes in
about ten waves whether the system has twenty compute nodes or two
hundred. Duration therefore stops being a function of scale and
becomes a function of per-pod cycle time alone.

Template updateStrategy and minReadySeconds in the
pci-irq-affinity-agent chart. It emitted no updateStrategy at all, so
the rendered object fell back to the Kubernetes default of
maxUnavailable: 1 and no override could reach it. The failure mode was
silent: an override was accepted and displayed by helm-override-show
while the rendered DaemonSet stayed unchanged. The chart defaults are
left at max_unavailable: 1, so the template change alone is
behaviour-neutral and only makes the value reachable; the value itself
comes from the static overrides.

Set disableWait to false on libvirt, openvswitch,
pci-irq-affinity-agent and nova. With the rollouts now fitting the
existing 30m timeout, the wait no longer causes the failure it was
introduced to avoid. The deployed helm-controller uses the kstatus
poller wait strategy, which already treats a DaemonSet as current only
when the observed generation matches and updatedNumberScheduled equals
desiredNumberScheduled, so no custom health-check expressions are
needed to make the wait correct.

Because a percentage rounds up with a floor of one, systems with one
or two compute nodes resolve to 1 and behave exactly as before, so no
special case is needed for AIO configurations. Absolute concurrency
does grow with node count, which is deliberate: 10% is two nodes at
twenty and twenty nodes at two hundred.

The neutron agents are left at max_unavailable: 1. Their largest host
group completes in about 16 minutes at that setting, so they were
never at risk, and raising them would not reduce the interaction
described below. The ceilometer release keeps disableWait: true: its
compute DaemonSet does not exist on the currently supported update
source, so on that path it is a fresh install rather than a rolling
update, maxUnavailable does not govern DaemonSet creation, and waiting
on 102 simultaneous pod creations has not been characterised. The
eight non-DaemonSet releases that also carry disableWait: true are
untouched; they predate this defect and their reasons are not
recorded, so each needs its own assessment.

Readiness and liveness probe settings are unchanged, min_ready_seconds
stays at 0, no HelmRelease timeout or interval value changes, and no
dependsOn ordering is added. The Deployment rolling-update path is
untouched; its replica counts track controllers rather than compute
nodes and it has no equivalent exposure.

One behavioural consequence should be recorded. Restarting an
openvswitch pod interrupts instance network connectivity on that node
for roughly three seconds, because the OVS kernel datapath keeps
forwarding on cached flows while ovs-vswitchd restarts. That cost is
per-node and is already paid on every application update today; this
change does not increase it, but it does compress those interruptions
from hours into minutes. Separately, when a node's openvswitch and
neutron-ovs-agent pods are replaced within about sixteen seconds of
each other, the datapath loses userspace flow state while the agent
that would reprogram it is unavailable, and connectivity is
interrupted for 25 to 30 seconds instead. Measured on roughly 11% of
nodes at these values. Ordering the openvswitch and neutron releases
would remove that coincidence and is proposed separately.

Test Plan:

Standard configuration, 2 controllers, 102 openstack-labelled compute
nodes, 500 running instances. Rollout duration and concurrency:
  PASS - libvirt full rollout in 11m45s at 11 concurrent, against a
         predicted 12.3m
  PASS - openvswitch full rollout in 17m47s at 11 concurrent, against
         a predicted 20.8m
  PASS - pci-irq-affinity-agent full rollout in 18m32s at 11
         concurrent, against a predicted 21.2m
  PASS - nova-compute full rollout in 5m36s, 7 concurrent on its
         largest host group and 14 across all seven
  PASS - all four charts complete inside the 30m HelmRelease timeout
  PASS - per-pod cycle time does not degrade with concurrency;
         measured wave intervals were below the single-replacement
         baseline on every chart
  PASS - all 500 instances remain ACTIVE throughout every rollout

Percentage resolution, same configuration:
  PASS - a 102-pod DaemonSet resolves 10% to 11
  PASS - an 8-pod host group resolves 10% to 1, confirming round-up
         with a floor of one
  PASS - a 14-pod host group resolves 10% to 2
  PASS - percentage accepted as a string by the IntOrString field

pci-irq-affinity-agent chart rendering:
  PASS - renders maxUnavailable: 1 as an integer from the default
  PASS - renders maxUnavailable: 10% as a string from the override
  PASS - omits updateStrategy and minReadySeconds when the entry is
         disabled
  PASS - omits the rollingUpdate block when pod_replacement_strategy
         is not RollingUpdate
  PASS - rendered output byte-identical to the pre-change chart when
         defaults are used
  PASS - the static override reaches the rendered DaemonSet, which the
         chart could not do before

Instance impact, probed by TCP connect at sub-second resolution:
  PASS - libvirt, zero failed connections across 52481 samples during
         a full rollout
  PASS - pci-irq-affinity-agent, zero failed connections across 83221
         samples during a full rollout
  PASS - openvswitch, interruption of 2.2 to 3.8 seconds per node on
         bare-metal nodes, one occurrence per node, matching the
         single-replacement baseline
  FAIL* - openvswitch concurrent with neutron-ovs-agent, interruption
         of 25 to 30 seconds on nodes where both pods are replaced
         within about sixteen seconds

Status accuracy, same configuration:
  <TO BE COMPLETED FROM THE UPGRADE RUN — see the four items below>
  - each affected release reports READY=True only after its DaemonSet
    reports updatedNumberScheduled equal to desiredNumberScheduled
  - sysinv reports the application applying until every DaemonSet
    rollout has completed

charts already have. It is safe in every supported configuration:
libvirt has no _is_enabled override and never removes its own

edge also holds with nova on disableWait: true, because dependsOn gates

parallelised should go unwatched. libvirt and pci-irq-affinity-agent

overlaps neutron's fifteen minutes and roughly one node is affected,
but compressed to about eighteen minutes nearly every node's
replacement falls inside neutron's window, and the figure measured at
102-node scale was about 11%. Ordering the two releases removes the
interaction rather than reducing its probability, so scaling this chart
is deferred to the change that lands that ordering.

The neutron release is unchanged and carries only a comment, for two
separate reasons. A dependsOn entry naming openvswitch cannot be
declared: when OVS runs with DPDK the dataplane is managed on the host
and the openvswitch chart is not deployed at all, because

execute_kustomize_updates hook in the neutron plugin, neither of which
exists yet.

they fit the timeout. The largest agent group on the measured system is
62 pods, about 16.5 minutes, but only because its 102 nodes split into
nested and bare-metal host groups; on a homogeneous 100-node system

declared as post-install and post-upgrade Helm hooks, and

left out until the hook coupling is addressed.

The remaining releases that carry disableWait: true are untouched.

so each of the others needs its own assessment.

liveness probe settings are unchanged and min_ready_seconds stays at 0.
The Deployment rolling-update path is untouched; its replica counts
track controllers rather than compute nodes and it has no equivalent
exposure. Because a percentage rounds up with a floor of one, systems
with one or two compute nodes resolve to 1 and behave exactly as

concurrency does grow with node count, which is deliberate: 10% is two

Signed-off-by: ssajeev <sravan.sajeev@windriver.com>

Scale libvirt and pci-irq-affinity-agent DaemonSet rollouts

Every DaemonSet-bearing chart in the application pins
max_unavailable: 1, so a rolling update replaces pods one node at a
time and rollout duration grows linearly with the number of
openstack-labelled compute nodes. At 102-node scale libvirt takes
about 2h06m and openvswitch was measured at 3h07m on a serial
rollback. Each HelmRelease carries a 30m timeout, so these releases
can only be made to succeed by setting disableWait: true. Raising the
timeout only relocates the wall, because the duration stays
proportional to node count.

That workaround creates a second and worse problem. Flux reports a
release with disableWait: true as Ready as soon as the manifests are
accepted, before any pod has been replaced. Because sysinv treats the
HelmRelease Ready condition as its source of truth, the application is
reported applied and the apply-in-progress alarm is cleared while pods
are still cycling. The documented verification step of checking that
HelmReleases report READY=True passes in that state, so it does not
detect an incomplete rollout. The semantic checks that reject
host-unlock and host-swact during an apply are released at the same
moment, so those operations are accepted while replacements are still
in flight. A pod that fails to start or crash-loops during the rollout
is not surfaced as a release failure, because nothing is waiting on
readiness.

Fix both together on the charts where it can be done safely, since the
second cannot be fixed without the first.

Express max_unavailable as 10% on libvirt and pci-irq-affinity-agent,
and set disableWait to false on both. Kubernetes resolves a DaemonSet
maxUnavailable percentage by rounding up against
status.desiredNumberScheduled [1], so the wave count becomes ceil(1/p)
and is independent of node count: either chart completes in about ten
waves whether the system has twenty compute nodes or two hundred.
libvirt drops from 2h06m to 11m45s, which fits inside the existing 30m
timeout, so the wait no longer causes the failure it was introduced to
avoid. Both the kstatus poller strategy and Helm's built-in readiness
check treat a DaemonSet as ready only when the observed generation
matches and updatedNumberScheduled and numberReady equal
desiredNumberScheduled [3], so the wait is correct under either
strategy and no custom health-check expressions are needed.

These two charts are the ones where parallelising is safe, because
their pods are node-local. Neither holds state that another chart's
pods depend on mid-rollout, so replacing eleven at once is eleven
independent restarts rather than a fleet-wide event. Instance
connectivity is not carried by either: measured across a full rollout,
libvirt produced zero failed TCP connections in 52481 samples and
pci-irq-affinity-agent zero in 83221.

Template updateStrategy and minReadySeconds in the
pci-irq-affinity-agent chart. It emitted no updateStrategy at all, so
the rendered object fell back to the Kubernetes default of
maxUnavailable: 1 and no override could reach it. The failure mode was
silent: an override was accepted and displayed by helm-override-show
while the rendered DaemonSet stayed unchanged. The chart default is
left at max_unavailable: 1, so the template change alone is
behaviour-neutral and only makes the value reachable; the value itself
comes from the static overrides.

Express max_unavailable as 10% on ceilometer without changing its
disableWait. This value has no effect on the currently supported
update source, where the compute DaemonSet does not exist and is
therefore created rather than rolled. It is set here because recovery
applies the charts of the release being recovered to, so the value
shipped in this release paces both the next forward rollout and a
rollback into this release: roughly three hours of the application
being reported applied while pods cycle at 1, against under twenty
minutes at 10%. It cannot breach a timeout, because this release keeps
disableWait: true and nothing waits on the rollout.

Declare libvirt as a dependency of the nova release. nova-compute's
init container already lists a same-host libvirt pod with
requireSameNode: true, so without this edge the two releases are
unordered siblings under placement, Flux reconciles them concurrently,
and a nova pod can land on a node whose libvirt pod is mid-replacement
and stall until it becomes ready. The edge makes the release graph
express a dependency the charts already have. It is safe in every
supported configuration because libvirt has no _is_enabled override
and never removes its own HelmRelease, so the target always exists
wherever nova is deployed, and it holds regardless of nova's own
disableWait because dependsOn gates on the dependency. Its cost is
that pci-irq-affinity-agent, which depends on nova, starts about
twelve minutes later.

The rule this establishes, and the one every release touched here now
satisfies: a DaemonSet release either waits and is parallelised, or
does not wait and stays serial. The combination shipped previously,
serial and not waiting, is the one that produces a multi-hour rollout
reported as complete on arrival.

Because a percentage rounds up with a floor of one, systems with one
or two compute nodes resolve to 1 and behave exactly as before, so no
special case is needed for AIO configurations. Absolute concurrency
does grow with node count, which is deliberate: 10% is two nodes at
twenty and twenty at two hundred.

openvswitch is deliberately left unscaled, and the reason is service
impact rather than timeout. Restarting an openvswitch pod interrupts
instance connectivity on that node for 2.2 to 3.8 seconds, because the
OVS kernel datapath keeps forwarding on cached flows while
ovs-vswitchd restarts. That cost is per-node and is already paid on
every update today. But when a node has its openvswitch and
neutron-ovs-agent pods replaced within about sixteen seconds of each
other, the datapath loses its userspace flow state while the agent
that would reprogram it is also unavailable, and connectivity is
interrupted for 25 to 30 seconds instead. Exposure is a function of
how much of the openvswitch rollout overlaps neutron's: at three hours
only a small part of the run overlaps neutron's fifteen minutes and
roughly one node is affected, but compressed to eighteen minutes
nearly every node's replacement falls inside neutron's window, and the
figure measured at 102-node scale was about 11%. Ordering the two
releases removes the interaction rather than reducing its probability,
so scaling this chart is deferred to the change that lands that
ordering.

A dependsOn from neutron to openvswitch is not that ordering, and this
change does not add one. When OVS runs with DPDK the dataplane is
managed on the host and the openvswitch chart is not deployed at all:
OpenvswitchHelm._is_enabled returns False and execute_kustomize_updates
then calls helm_release_resource_delete, removing the HelmRelease from
the kustomization. A dependsOn entry naming a HelmRelease that does
not exist leaves the dependent release permanently unreconciled, so
the application apply would never complete on a DPDK deployment. The
two conditions do not overlap, since the interaction requires a
containerised openvswitch pod, which is exactly the configuration in
which the dependency would be valid, so a conditional edge added under
the same predicate that governs the chart is correct rather than a
compromise. It needs a dependency-removal method alongside
helm_release_resource_delete in sysinv/helm/kustomize_base.py and an
execute_kustomize_updates hook in the neutron plugin, neither of which
exists yet. Both files carry comments recording this.

The neutron agents are left at max_unavailable: 1, and not because
they fit the timeout. Whether they fit is configuration-dependent: the
largest agent group on the measured system was 62 pods and finished in
about 16 minutes, but that system splits its compute nodes across
groups, and a homogeneous 100-node system puts all of them in one
group at roughly 35 minutes, which breaches the 30m timeout. The
durable reason is that unlike libvirt and pci-irq-affinity-agent the
neutron agents are not node-local in what they serve: l3-agent and
dhcp-agent own routers and networks, and with
max_l3_agents_per_router: 1 and l3_ha: false each router has exactly
one agent hosting it. Eleven concurrent replacements is therefore
eleven routers losing their only agent, not eleven independent
restarts. Scaling these needs per-agent treatment, which this change
does not attempt.

nova keeps disableWait: true and max_unavailable: 1. nova-db-sync and
nova-rabbit-init are declared as post-install and post-upgrade Helm
hooks, and nova-compute's init container lists both as
kubernetes-entrypoint dependencies. Helm runs the readiness wait
before the post-upgrade hook phase, so with disableWait: false the
newly created nova-compute pods block on jobs that Helm has not
created yet while Helm blocks on those pods, and the release deadlocks
until the timeout. This is scale-independent and would deadlock on a
single-node system, so nova can yield no status-accuracy improvement
until the hook coupling is addressed. Scaling it alone would only
shorten the window in which it is misreported, which is the property
this change is trying to remove rather than shorten, so it is left at
1 and the HelmRelease carries a comment recording the constraint. The
general form of the constraint: a DaemonSet may take
disableWait: false only if no init-container dependency resolves to a
resource created in that same release's post-upgrade hook phase.

The remaining releases carrying disableWait: true are untouched. Their
reasons predate this defect and are not recorded, nova and ceilometer
excepted, so each needs its own assessment.

Readiness and liveness probe settings are unchanged, min_ready_seconds
stays at 0, and no HelmRelease timeout or interval value changes. The
Deployment rolling-update path is untouched; its replica counts track
controllers rather than compute nodes and it has no equivalent
exposure.

usm: Relocate the etcd keyspace on a simplex platform upgrade

Before the fixed-first etcd design the single etcd member ('controller')
kept its data on the DRBD-backed path /opt/etcd/db/controller.etcd. This
release founds the cluster on a fixed member ('fixed-0') backed by local
disk at /opt/etcd-fixed/db/fixed-0.etcd.

On simplex there is no second member to replicate from, so the keyspace
has to be physically relocated during the upgrade. Without it the
upgraded system comes up on an empty datastore and every Kubernetes
object is lost.

Add upgrade script 203-simplex-etcd-keyspace-migration.py, registered in
the upgrade-scripts plugin runner. It takes a snapshot of the N-1
floating data directory and restores it into the fixed member data
directory, naming the member and its cluster-host peer URL so the
resulting directory describes a single-member cluster.

The script is guarded to simplex and is a no-op elsewhere, deliberately.
Per HLD section 11.3 the fixed members on duplex are added to the still
running floating cluster with 'etcdctl member add' and populate
themselves through Raft replication; that is what
add_fixed_etcd_members_for_upgrade() does, dispatched by the periodic
membership audit on DEPLOY_STATE_ACTIVATE. Restoring a snapshot there
would seed fixed-0 as its own cluster with its own cluster ID, which
could then never join the existing one.

The script is idempotent, guarded by the marker file
/etc/platform/.etcd_upgrade_data_migrated, and fails safe: the original
floating data directory is left untouched, so a failed migration can be
retried or rolled back without data loss.

Closes-Bug: CGTS-103691
Test-Plan: WRCPPV-11160

Before the fixed-first etcd design the single etcd member ('controller')
kept its data on the DRBD-backed path /opt/etcd/db/controller.etcd. This
release founds the cluster on a fixed member ('fixed-0') backed by local
disk at /opt/etcd-fixed/db/fixed-0.etcd.

On simplex there is no second member to replicate from, so the keyspace
has to be physically relocated during the upgrade. Without it the
upgraded system comes up on an empty datastore and every Kubernetes
object is lost.

Add upgrade script 203-simplex-etcd-keyspace-migration.py, registered in
the upgrade-scripts plugin runner. It takes a snapshot of the N-1
floating data directory and restores it into the fixed member data
directory, naming the member and its cluster-host peer URL so the
resulting directory describes a single-member cluster.

The script is guarded to simplex and is a no-op elsewhere, deliberately.
Per HLD section 11.3 the fixed members on duplex are added to the still
running floating cluster with 'etcdctl member add' and populate
themselves through Raft replication; that is what
add_fixed_etcd_members_for_upgrade() does, dispatched by the periodic
membership audit on DEPLOY_STATE_ACTIVATE. Restoring a snapshot there
would seed fixed-0 as its own cluster with its own cluster ID, which
could then never join the existing one.

The script is idempotent, guarded by the marker file
/etc/platform/.etcd_upgrade_data_migrated, and fails safe: the original
floating data directory is left untouched, so a failed migration can be
retried or rolled back without data loss.

Closes-Bug: CGTS-103691
Test-Plan: WRCPPV-11160
Depends-On: https://review.opendev.org/c/starlingx/stx-puppet/+/998118

The floating instance is also taken out of service. The N-1 release ran
etcd as an SM-managed service on the DRBD-backed path; on this release a
simplex system runs only the fixed instance, so the floating service is
unmanaged by SM and disabled in systemd once the keyspace has moved.
Left in place it would contend for the client and peer ports, be
restarted by SM, and on the next boot start against a data directory
that is no longer the cluster's.

usm: relocate etcd keyspace on simplex upgrade

On simplex the etcd keyspace lives on the DRBD-backed path used by the
floating instance. The fixed-first design runs a single local-disk member
instead, so the data has to move before that member starts, or it founds an
empty cluster on the new data directory and the keyspace is lost with
nothing reporting a failure.

Relocate the keyspace during activate: mount the DRBD device if it is not
already mounted, restore the snapshot into the fixed member's data
directory, render the environment file to match, then start the member and
verify it serves the restored data before the upgrade proceeds.

The hash check is skipped on restore. The snapshot is taken from a live
member rather than written by snapshot save, so it carries no integrity
hash and etcdutl refuses it without the flag.

Duplex needs no equivalent. There the fixed members join a running cluster
and replicate through raft, so the data arrives without being moved.

Test Plan:
  PASS  simplex upgrade relocates the keyspace to the fixed member's data
        directory and the member serves it
  PASS  keys written before the upgrade read back unchanged after activate
  PASS  a second activate is a no-op
  PASS  duplex upgrade unaffected

revisions.message:
mariadb: Back up locally on the configured host

Kolla Ansible runs the backup container on mariadb_backup_host and
mounts the MariaDB data and backup volumes from that host.

However, the replica backup script discovers a database server through
the load balancer and may connect to a different Galera node.
Mariabackup then reads database metadata from the remote node while
reading /var/lib/mysql from the local container host. This can cause LSN
mismatches and make the backup stall.

Use the local Unix socket for both full and incremental backups. Remove
the replica-specific script so that the database connection, data files,
and backup output always belong to the host running the backup
container.

Closes-Bug: #2141558
Related: blueprint database-backup-recovery

NetApp ONTAP REST: restore snapshot-dir fallback for CG clones

Restores two code paths dropped when patch 993363 was split to remove
its bug-fix portion:

* nfs_cmode.py stopped passing source_snapshot to clone_file(), so NFS
  CG-snapshot clones silently sourced from the live file instead of
  the snapshot.
* client_cmode_rest.py's clone_lun()/clone_file() lost the
  snapshot_directory_access_enabled check and private-CLI fallback, so
  clones failed outright when that FlexVol setting is False.

Restores get_volume_snapshot_dir_access(), _clone_via_private_cli(),
_clone_lun_via_private_cli(), _check_lun_visible(), the fallback
branching in clone_lun()/clone_file(), and their unit tests.

Verified live on a real ONTAP cluster: iSCSI and NFS CG-snapshot clones
now succeed with snapshot_directory_access_enabled both True and
False, and the NFS clone log shows the real snapshot id instead of
None.

revisions.message:
etcd: add certificate reissue and fix member-add guard for SX-to-DX

The simplex-to-duplex migration path fails on the first duplex unlock
because of two issues in the etcd puppet code:

1. Certificate SAN mismatch: At simplex bootstrap the etcd server
   certificate only carries the cluster-host floating address in its
   Subject Alternative Name set. After conversion the membership class
   rewrites etcd-fixed to bind the controller-0 unit address, and the
   TLS handshake fails because the certificate does not cover it.

   Fix: add platform::etcd::certificates, a puppet class that calls
   etcd_duplex_migration.py --certificates to reissue the certificate
   with the full SAN set (floating + both unit addresses + loopback).
   The class is ordered after platform::network writes /etc/hosts and
   before platform::etcd::membership restarts etcd-fixed. An unless
   guard makes it a no-op when the SAN set is already correct (fresh
   duplex bootstrap).

2. Member-add unless guard: The migration playbook registers the
   floating etcd member as a learner before the unlock. At unlock
   puppet tries to add it again. The unless guard greps for the member
   name ('controller'), but an unstarted learner has an empty name
   field in 'etcdctl member list' output -- only the peer URL is
   present. The grep fails, puppet runs the add, etcd returns "Peer
   URLs already exists", and controllerconfig fails.

   Fix: extend the unless guard to also match the floating peer URL
   so it catches both started (by name) and unstarted (by URL) members.

Test Plan:
- AIO-SX to AIO-DX migration with etcd-ha-controlplane topic
- Verified controller-0 boots into duplex mode after unlock
- Verified etcd cluster has 2 members (fixed-0 + controller/floating)
- Verified fresh duplex bootstrap is unaffected (certificates class skips)

revisions.message:
Allow shrinking a segment range to an allocated boundary

Updating a network segment range to reduce its minimum or maximum was
rejected as referenced by a tenant network even when every allocated
segment still fell within the requested new range. The guard against
stranding allocated segments used inclusive comparisons (>= and <=),
so a new boundary that landed exactly on the lowest or highest
allocated segment was wrongly treated as impacting them.

Use strict comparisons so the update is only blocked when the new
minimum rises above the lowest allocated segment or the new maximum
drops below the highest allocated segment.

Depends-On: https://review.opendev.org/c/openstack/neutron-tempest-plugin/+/1000364
Closes-Bug: #2161678

Change-Id: Ibc51c722669f3ea9b16d6821554d92fcb5f924c3
Signed-off-by: Doug Goldstein <cardoe@cardoe.com>
(cherry picked from commit 0ea814f6a41d6fa39fad6a68d57af68bbe89a589)

collectd ptp: log per-pin DPLL state from dpll-mgr status.json

Add per-pin state and priority logging to the dpll-mgr audit cycle.
Each configured pin is logged on its own line, matching the existing
key=value style used for other status.json fields.

  dpll-mgr dpll-mgr1 pin GNSS_REF4P state=connected priority=0
  dpll-mgr dpll-mgr1 pin SDP0_REF0N state=selectable priority=12

disconnected, or active directly from collectd.log without needing
to read status.json or enable dpll-mgr debug logging.

revisions.message:
sysinv: apply the control-plane endpoint manifest after unlock

Move controlPlaneEndpoint from the kube-apiserver port onto the HAProxy
load balancer after unlock. Bootstrap points it at kube-apiserver directly
because HAProxy is configured by the unlock manifest and started by Service
Manager, so nothing listens on :6443 while kubeadm init runs.

Apply it from iplatform_update_by_ihost() on the first-report-available
path, immediately after the etcd runtime manifest. The same guards apply:
controller personality, non-simplex, initial config complete.

This also covers the other lifecycle paths without a separate hook:
- simplex-to-duplex: the script returns early on simplex, picks up on
  the first unlock as duplex
- upgrade/rollback: each unlock re-applies, no-op when already correct
- restore: reconciles from whatever the backup captured

revisions.message:
Support pushing to registered Gerrit servers

M5 of the multi-Gerrit series: extend the workspace/push layer
(opendev_mcp/patch.py) so create_change/revise_change/replace_change
can push against any registered (non-default) Gerrit server, not just
the identity's default one.

- PushTarget (patch.py) is the lightweight, non-I/O descriptor the
  push functions now accept alongside GerritAccount; push_target_for()
  projects a ProfileStore.resolve_gerrit_server() result onto it. The
  default-server path (GerritAccount + workspace.ensure_source_clone)
  is completely untouched.
- SSH mode: the remote embeds the network-boundary-vetted IP
  (resolve_public_host, resolved once per push and reused throughout —
  never re-resolved mid-push), with -o HostKeyAlias=<host[:port]> so
  known_hosts verification stays keyed by hostname. known_hosts content
  comes from the gerrit_servers row's pinned ssh_host_keys, written to
  a per-invocation 0600 file; a NULL ssh_host_keys refuses the push
  with a clear "refresh host keys" error (no TOFU at push time).
- HTTP mode: the remote embeds the username only; the password travels
  via a GIT_ASKPASS helper (a static, secret-free 0700 script per
  invocation) reading OPENDEV_MCP_GIT_USERNAME/PASSWORD from the
  subprocess env — never argv, the URL, or git config. Every
  network-touching git call is pinned via http.curloptResolve, applied
  through GIT_CONFIG_COUNT/KEY_0/VALUE_0 env vars rather than an argv
  -c flag so it also reaches git-review's own internal `git push`
  subprocess. A git-version gate refuses HTTP-mode pushes on a git
  older than 2.31 (curloptResolve support), since an old git would
  silently ignore the pin and connect unpinned.
- Per-server git_fullname/git_email (already resolved by
  ResolvedGerritServer) thread through the existing identity-env
  mechanism; _git_identity_env now accepts either account-ish type.
- known_hosts_host_field is lifted from identities_api.py into
  accounts.py (shared, pure) so both the M4 keyscan-pinning path and
  this module's ssh pinning use one definition.
- identities_api.py's POST .../gerrit-servers now runs a real soft SSH
  check (patch.soft_ssh_check) instead of always reporting "skipped",
  reusing the same pinned-connection plumbing and the address the
  keyscan step already vetted; response shape is unchanged
  ("ok" | "failed: <category>" | "skipped").

Tests: unit coverage for remote URL construction (both modes, IPv6),
GIT_SSH_COMMAND/GIT_ASKPASS/curloptResolve construction, askpass
execution (both prompts), file permissions (0600/0700), the
DNS-rebinding-defense "single resolution reused for the whole push"
behavior, netpolicy refusal propagation, missing-credential/host-key
errors, scratch-directory cleanup (including on early failure), a
password leak-hunt across every captured argv/env, per-server git
identity threading, the git-version gate, and soft_ssh_check's
ok/failed-category/skipped outcomes. tox -e pep8 and tox -e py3 pass
(1696 tests).

Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_012ojSQk2q3SG2LGr4D6xpNr

Round-9 fix: the next deterministic Zuul failure, one layer deeper
than the round-6/7 ones (Archon's CI diagnosis on 1001734 PS3): the
multi-Gerrit setup, credential verification, and reads all worked --
the first HTTP-mode gerrit_create_change then failed cloning
https://gate-gerrit/a/gate/sandbox/ with git/libcurl rejecting the
fixture certificate ("certificate signer not trusted", using
/etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt, git's OWN default bundle).
httpx (this module's own REST clients, and the console door's OIDC
discovery) honors SSL_CERT_FILE natively for its trust store, but
git's own HTTPS transport (libcurl) does not -- it needs
GIT_SSL_CAINFO (env) or http.sslCAInfo (config) to trust anything
beyond its compiled-in default, and _env_for_target (which owns the
git subprocess env construction for HTTP-mode targets) never threaded
SSL_CERT_FILE through to it.

Fixed generically, not as gate-only plumbing: when the gateway
process's own environment carries SSL_CERT_FILE, _env_for_target now
also sets GIT_SSL_CAINFO to that same path for HTTP-mode targets,
unless GIT_SSL_CAINFO is already present in the process env (an
operator who set it explicitly -- deliberately a different trust
store just for git -- wins over the inference). Documented in the
function's own docstring as the general production behavior it is:
an operator pointing the whole gateway at a private-CA Gerrit via
SSL_CERT_FILE now gets git trusting the same store httpx already
does, not just REST calls. Checked DEPLOYMENT.md/README.rst/doc/ for
any existing SSL_CERT_FILE documentation to extend with a one-line
git-follows-it-too note -- none exists (SSL_CERT_FILE is currently
gate-only plumbing, never operator-documented), so no doc section was
invented.

Round-10 fix (Archon, on both 1001707 PS7 and 1001721 PS9, replacing
his prior +1 on this change -- a production-path blocker, not gate
plumbing): create_change's Change-Id stamping relied ENTIRELY on the
commit-msg hook installed by `git review -s`
(workspace.ensure_source_clone / _ensure_source_clone_for_target,
both already best-effort/non-fatal by design). That install can fail
silently: a registered Gerrit whose advertised hook-download URL
differs from the address this module actually reaches it on (the gate
fixture's 127.0.0.1:8083, unreachable from inside the gateway
container, is the concrete case found; any real Gerrit with a
canonical-vs-reachable URL mismatch has the identical shape) leaves
.git/hooks/commit-msg never installed. The old
`git rebase --exec 'git commit --amend --no-edit'` depended wholly on
that hook firing to add anything, so with none installed it was a
pure no-op -- a commit could reach the real Gerrit with NO Change-Id
trailer at all, which Gerrit rejects server-side ("missing Change-Id
in message footer"). Both account types funnel through this one
function, so the old design's vulnerability was shared, not
registered-server-specific.

Fixed with independent, hook-free Change-Id generation plus a
fail-closed invariant check (Archon's own "second option," explicitly
preferred over merely making the hook install more reliable):
_stamp_change_ids_over_range's rebase --exec step now runs a small,
self-contained script (_CHANGE_ID_STAMP_SCRIPT) instead of a bare
`git commit --amend --no-edit`: it still gives a real installed hook
the first chance to fire (free when present, a no-op when it isn't),
then checks HEAD's message directly and, if a Change-Id is still
missing, generates one locally by hashing the same shape of input
Gerrit's own hook hashes (tree + parent + author + committer +
message, fed to `git hash-object -t commit` as a synthetic commit
object) and amends it in -- no hook, no network, dependent on nothing
but the commit's own already-committed content. Commits that already
carry a Change-Id (from a working hook, or because the input already
had one) are left completely untouched, verbatim; exact byte-parity
with the real hook's own message-cleaning rules was deliberately not
attempted -- only the I<40-hex> shape and per-commit uniqueness are
required, and both are guaranteed by construction. A new
_verify_change_ids_over_range, called by create_change right after
stamping and before anything is collected/pushed, is the fail-closed
invariant Archon asked for: every commit about to be pushed must carry
EXACTLY ONE well-formed Change-Id trailer, or a specific internal
PatchError is raised before git-review (and the real Gerrit) ever see
it. It should never actually fire -- stamping guarantees the invariant
on its own -- but turns a hypothetical future regression into an
immediate, actionable error instead of an opaque server-side
rejection.

`git review -s` itself is left in place, unchanged, in
_ensure_source_clone_for_target: it was already best-effort/non-fatal
before this fix and stays that way after it -- the smallest honest
change, since ripping it out would trade a working, harmless call (and
the existing TestEnsureSourceCloneForTargetTempCleanupOnException
regression coverage built around it) for no behavioral gain now that
Change-Id stamping no longer depends on whether it ever succeeds; its
own docstring and log message now say so explicitly. The default
server path (workspace.ensure_source_clone) shares the identical
best-effort hook-install shape and was therefore equally vulnerable
before this fix -- both are covered by the same one fix, in the one
function (_stamp_change_ids_over_range) both create_change flows
already funnel through, with no per-path duplication needed.

tests/gate/check_multi_gerrit_tools.py needed no functional changes:
its create-change assertions read change_numbers/diffstat/file_hashes
and the pushed commit's committer via anonymous REST, never anything
Change-Id-shaped, so nothing there assumed hook-based stamping.

Tests (real git throughout, not mocked calls):
_stamp_change_ids_over_range/_verify_change_ids_over_range exercised
against a repo with NO commit-msg hook installed at all (simulating a
failed/absent `git review -s` hook install): every commit in a
multi-commit stack gets a valid I<40-hex> Change-Id, distinct per
commit; a pre-existing Change-Id (as revise/replace's
_set_head_change_id already guaranteed, and as a create mbox whose tip
was stamped by a working hook would carry) is preserved verbatim, not
regenerated; the same stamp-then-verify sequence run against a real
format-patch mbox applied via git am (mirroring create_change's own
strip -> am -> stamp order) end to end; and the fail-closed verifier
raises PatchError naming the exact wrong count for a commit missing a
trailer and for one carrying two, and stays silent once a stack is
properly stamped. Every new test was confirmed to fail against the
pre-fix hook-only stamping (git commit --amend --no-edit alone) before
being accepted. tox -e pep8 and tox -e py3 pass (1752 tests).

Add UNSYNC operating status for replicas

Docker health checks report database availability but do not show
whether a replica is still synchronized with its source.

Run an optional datastore-specific replication health check from the
existing guest-agent status periodic task. Report UNSYNC when
replication is stopped or the configured lag tolerance is exceeded,
while keeping the database available for instance actions.

only use the last replay timestamp while disconnected. Treat a missing
timestamp as UNSYNC, covering replicas that can no longer replay the
required WAL after rebuild.

revisions.message:
kernel: enable in-tree Intel FPGA (DFL/OPAE) support

Enable the in-tree Device Feature List (DFL) stack in both kernel-rt and
kernel-std configs so that Intel FPGA / OPAE cards (e.g. Intel PAC N3000)
are supported by the mainline drivers, without relying on the
out-of-tree opae-intel-fpga-driver DKMS package.

The OOT OPAE 2.0.1 driver mapped onto the upstream DFL framework
(drivers/fpga/dfl*) plus the MAX10 BMC, SPI, MTD and regmap pieces it
depends on. Enable the full chain as modules:

- FPGA core: FPGA, FPGA_BRIDGE, FPGA_REGION and the DFL bus
  (FPGA_DFL, FPGA_DFL_FME{,_MGR,_BRIDGE,_REGION}, FPGA_DFL_AFU,
  FPGA_DFL_PCI, FPGA_DFL_NIOS_INTEL_PAC_N3000, FPGA_M10_BMC_SEC_UPDATE)
  plus the Altera/Xilinx/Lattice/Microchip managers and bridges.
- MAX10 BMC: MFD_INTEL_M10_BMC_CORE/_SPI/_PMCI and
  SENSORS_INTEL_M10_BMC_HWMON.
- Buses/flash used by the above: REGMAP_SPI_AVMM, SPI_MEM,
  SPI_ALTERA{,_CORE,_DFL}, SPI_INTEL{,_PCI,_PLATFORM}, MTD_SPI_NOR.

The config change is identical for kernel-rt and kernel-std to keep both
flavours aligned. New collateral symbols surfaced by enabling the above
(SERIAL_8250_DFL, PTP_DFL_TOD, SPI_ZYNQMP_GQSPI, SPI_AMD) are left at
their disabled defaults.

In addition, backport the OPAE image_load sysfs interface that mainline
does not carry:

- fpga/0001-fpga-m10bmc-sec-add-image_load-sysfs-for-N3000-and-D.patch:
  the mainline MAX10 BMC secure-update driver exposes only the
  firmware-upload ABI and lacks the control/available_images and
  control/image_load attributes OPAE userspace uses to trigger an RSU
  or retimer firmware reload. Add the N3000 and D5005 subset (bmc_user,
  bmc_factory, and retimer_fw for N3000), ported from linux-dfl commits
  e1b885714f68 and 604ad4f48cee, along with the M10BMC_PKVL_POLL_CTRL
  register definitions in intel-m10-bmc.h needed by the retimer path.
  N6000/PMCI/SDM handlers are intentionally left out; the N6000 ops keep
  .image_load = NULL so the control/ group stays hidden for them.

The patch is applied to both kernel-rt and kernel-std.

Verification:
- Build kernel and out of tree modules success for rt and std.
- Build iso success for rt and std.
- Install success onto a lab with std kernel, and can switch to rt.
- Boot up successfully in the lab; DFL/FPGA modules load and the
  FPGA devices enumerate.
- On Intel PAC N3000, control/available_images reports
  "bmc_factory bmc_user retimer_fw" and image_load accepts a valid name.
- The sanity testing was run and the test results PASS.

kernel: add OPAE SDK userspace package for Debian trixie

Add a new userspace package, userspace/opae-sdk, that builds the Intel
OPAE SDK 2.14.0-3 for the Debian trixie layer. This is the userspace
companion to the in-tree Intel FPGA (DFL/OPAE) kernel enablement: it
provides the OPAE runtime, the development files and the extra FPGA
tools used to manage Intel FPGA / OPAE cards (e.g. Intel PAC N3000).

The source is the upstream release tarball
(https://github.com/OFS/opae-sdk/archive/refs/tags/2.14.0-3.zip). As it
is a .zip whose top-level directory is opae-sdk-2.14.0-3, a dl_hook
unzips it and renames the tree to <debname>-<debver> (opae-2.14.0-3),
mirroring the existing kernel-modules/intel-opae-fpga zip handling.

The Debian packaging under debian/trixie/deb_folder is derived from the
upstream packaging/opae/deb tree and adapted for the trixie toolchain:

- control: Maintainer switched to StarlingX, debhelper-compat (= 13),
  and the Build-Depends completed for an out-of-the-box build:
  pkg-config, pybind11-dev, libcli11-dev, libspdlog-dev and libnuma-dev
  (OPAE would otherwise FetchContent these, which debhelper disables),
  python3-jsonschema and python3-yaml (needed by the build-time
  ofs_parse.py generator), plus python3-pip/setuptools/wheel for the
  OPAE_BUILD_PYTHON_DIST stage.
- rules: set DEB_BUILD_OPTIONS=noddebs; reference the out-of-tree cmake
  build dir as obj-$(DEB_HOST_GNU_TYPE) instead of a hardcoded arch;
  pip-install the python dist artifacts with --break-system-packages and
  DEB_PYTHON_INSTALL_LAYOUT=deb_system so they land under /usr and
  dist-packages (PEP 668 / trixie). OPAE's cmake also stages those
  python packages under /usr/local, so the duplicate /usr/local tree is
  removed before packaging.
- opae-devel.install: add the cmake package-config exports
  (usr/lib/opae-2.14.0/*.cmake and modules/*.cmake) and the top-level
  usr/include/opae/cxx/core.h header, and resolve the @VERSION@
  placeholder in opae-devel.dirs to 2.14.0.

The package is registered for the trixie std build in
debian_trixie_pkg_dirs_std, and the three resulting binary packages
(opae, opae-devel, opae-extra-tools) are added to
debian_trixie_iso_image_std.inc.

Test Plan:
Pass: downloader - dl_hook unzips and renames to opae-2.14.0-3
Pass: build opae, opae-devel and opae-extra-tools (Debian trixie,
      debian:13, amd64)
Pass: dpkg-deb metadata sane - versions 2.14.0-3, opae-devel depends
      opae (= 2.14.0-3), opae-extra-tools depends opae + opae-devel,
      shlib dependencies auto-resolved
Pass: no dh_missing failures - runtime libraries/binaries, headers and
      FPGA tools present in the expected packages

revisions.message:
Adapt served map fragments to layer specs

Phase 6 of the API repo's doc/plans/mapstyle-architecture.md begins:
clients stop building map style, servers serve it. The API now
composes each user's track sources and layers from the grouping
constants and their tile files, so this app's paint, layout and base
filter builders have a replacement waiting for them.

This change is the pure addition that makes the flip possible, not
the flip itself. api.ts learns the two fragment endpoints, reusing
the grouping conversion the grouping endpoints already apply rather
than growing a second answer to what shape a grouping is. The new
map/fragment-adapter.ts reshapes a served document into the same
TileSourceLayerSpec/TrackLayerSpec values WanderTracksMap.syncTracks
and the editor's applier consume today, so the follow-up host change
is a swap of one builder for another and nothing else moves.

What stays client-side is only what is dynamic: which groupings are
switched on, and whose vehicles' tracks are wanted. The vehicle
clause of buildGroupingFilter is ported over verbatim, including the
never-true expression that means "nothing selected draws nothing",
and composed onto the served base filter rather than into it - the
expression is the API's to own now.

The tests drive the adapter with a document generated by running the
API's own mapfragments.py over two tile files and the fourteen
groupings, so what they pin is the contract rather than a
restatement of it. The bundled tile file's id is a UUID on purpose:
layer ids are track-{tilefile}-{grouping} and the tile file half
contains hyphens, so the split matches the served grouping ids
instead of guessing at separators.

revisions.message:
Fail CI when vendored basemaps drift

app/src/main/assets/basemaps holds copies of the API repo's
wandertracks/mapstyles -- the same style JSON the API serves at
/api/v1/styles/<basemap>.json, carried in the APK so a device that
cannot reach the API renders the same map it would have gotten
online. They were hand-synced, and BasemapStyleProvider's own
comment said so. Hand-synced cross-repo copies are precisely the
drift the mapstyle-centralization effort exists to kill: the
failure mode is silent, only visible on a phone that happens to be
offline, and arbitrarily long after the API-side edit that caused
it.

So add wandertracks-android-basemap-parity, running the assets
against the API repo's originals in a required-projects checkout.
It is not a child of wandertracks-android-base -- the check is a
python3 stdlib script over parsed JSON, needing neither the SDK nor
Gradle -- and it carries no files matcher, because a drift detector
that only runs when someone touched the assets cannot catch the
change that forgot to. required-projects also makes Depends-On work
across the repos, so a style edit upstream and the asset refresh
here gate together.

Parity is asserted on the parsed JSON rather than the bytes,
because exactly two differences are legitimate. Serialization: the
API repo's files are pretty-printed for human review, the assets
are compact because the phone parses them rather than reading them.
Key order: nothing on either side depends on it. Everything else
fails, including the {{ESRI_API_TOKEN}} placeholder, which is the
on-disk form on both sides -- the API substitutes it at serve time
and BasemapStyleProvider at load time, so a real token appearing in
either tree is drift and comparing the placeholder text verbatim is
what catches it.

All five styles are in sync today; this pins that. The script takes
the two directories as arguments and defaults to the side-by-side
checkout layout, so it runs locally as well as in the job, and it
exits non-zero rather than skipping when it cannot find one side --
a parity check that passes when it looked at nothing is worse than
no parity check.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_011AjEPaSLDfby8e86JG8xAe
Change-Id: Id582da261d195ddb056758c111183d99db91314d

revisions.message:
Retire the deprecated grouping endpoints

Track styling is derived once, server-side, and shipped to clients as
finished MapLibre sources and layers by the map-fragments endpoints.
The grouping endpoints existed only to feed the client-side layer
builders that composed those specs themselves: the web's builders are
gone, the styling editor page is gone, and Android never called them.
The same constants still reach clients, inside the fragments payload.

Removed: GET /api/v1/trackgroupings (namespace and module) and
GET /api/v1/public/u/{slug}/groupings with its response model.

The config endpoint's esri_api_token goes with them for the same
reason: it parameterized client-built basemap styles, and the API now
renders those styles itself, substituting the token when it serves
/api/v1/styles/<basemap>.json. That substitution keeps the default
token, which moves to styles.py alongside its only remaining reader;
WANDERTRACKS_ESRI_API_TOKEN still overrides it.

The unit test for the retired routes becomes an assertion that they
are absent from the URL map, so a re-registration is caught.
